title: Functional assessment of the educational needs of students with ASD in Bulgaria
abstract: Introduction. The increasing number of students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in mainstream schools necessitates the individualisation of educational pathways. The phenotypic heterogeneity of ASD manifestations presents challenges to traditional teaching methods, requiring a shift from the deficit-based medical model to the neurodiversity paradigm. Aim. The present study aims to differentiate the functional deficits and developmental resources of students with ASD in Bulgaria by applying the methodology of the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health for Children and Youth (ICF-CY), with the goal of designing an effective inclusive environment. Methodology and research methods. A cross-sectional observational study included 164 students with ASD, aged 3 to 19 years. Assessments were conducted by multidisciplinary teams of specialists through direct observation using an adapted “Functional Assessment Chart”. The textual data, consisting of free-form descriptions across nine criteria, were analysed using qualitative content analysis (semantic grouping) by three independent experts. Results. Twelve key factors contributing to a supportive environment were identified, including visualisation, structuring of the learning space, time management, and sensory safety. Qualitative analysis revealed that speech, behavioural, and cognitive difficulties tend to be mitigated when students’ strengths – such as visual and practical thinking and selective interests – are engaged. The data support the research hypothesis that targeted adaptation of environmental factors can reduce participation restrictions without relying solely on narrowly clinical interventions. Scientific novelty. For the first time in the Bulgarian educational context, the qualitative content of the functional profiles of students with ASD has been systematically categorised according to the ICF-CY framework. This approach goes beyond the traditional clinical description by embracing the neurodiversity paradigm, thereby highlighting the compensatory mechanisms involved in the child’s interaction with their environment. Practical significance. A practical algorithm and applied recommendations have been developed for mainstream teachers, specialists, and families to collaboratively design an inclusive and safe environment, as well as to conduct long-term, longitudinal monitoring of the child’s development.

title: From Multi-Agent Models to Enterprise Intelligent Agents: An AI-Powered Knowledge Compilation and Production Optimisation Platform for Oil and Gas Field Development
abstract: Oil and gas field development planning remains a slow, expert-dependent workflow, with multi-year plans scattered across subsidiaries in heterogeneous formats and tacit knowledge locked in individual experts. This paper presents an enterprise scientific research agent that compiles development plans into a unified knowledge base and enables autonomous scheme generation, simulation and continuous optimisation at enterprise scale. The architecture fuses a 240-indicator standardised ontology, multi-modal LLM knowledge compilation, a lifecycle-aware knowledge graph (facts, states, events), a RAG-augmented three-tier memory, long-horizon multi-agent orchestration (Build and Optimize modes with frozen-evidence acceptance), a unified MCP tool bus, and a git-style model relation tree that makes every run traceable and reversible. The platform has compiled 2,924 development plans across 14 subsidiaries of a national oil company. In a black-oil case, the agent autonomously generated water-flooding well-pattern schemes in two hours without human intervention, raising the ten-year recovery factor from 18.9% to 34.6% against a 30% target, while planning-cycle latency was substantially reduced. The results confirm that progressing from multi-agent research models to unified enterprise intelligent agents is a scalable path toward knowledge-driven decision-making in large, multi-asset petroleum portfolios.

title: AI-Agent-Built Fiber-Sensing Interpretation Platform for Real Well Operations
abstract: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) and distributed temperature sensing (DTS) are fiber-optic technologies that turn an optical fiber into a distributed sensor array. Originally developed in the telecommunications and defense sectors, these methods were adopted by the oil and gas industry. DTS entered thermal-recovery surveillance in the mid-1990s (Brown and Hartog 2002), and DAS followed more widely after the first downhole trials in 2009 (Molenaar et al. 2012). They now expand the observational basis for well logging by providing distributed temperature and acoustic measurements over the instrumented interval at survey-specific spatial and temporal sampling. However, interpretation-tool development has lagged acquisition technology: multiple vendor formats, multiday survey volumes, and job-specific processing still leave much of the acquired data underused relative to acquisition cost. An engineer-directed development approach was evaluated in which a domain engineer used general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents to construct a DAS/DTS and well-log interpretation software environment. Development was performed against field-surveillance data sets from multiple vendors and job types. As application scope increased, unstructured agent use was replaced by a documentation-driven operating framework comprising architecture rules, task-scoped guidance, decision ownership, plan-before-implementation, and automated numerical and regression checks. The implemented environment provided multiformat data access, stream-from-disk review of multiday surveys, synchronized visualization, deterministic processing, and restorable sessions. A first usable environment was completed within weeks and subsequently used to implement and evaluate two interpretation workflows across multiple surveys. For injection surveillance, channel-coherence processing, masked ridge extraction, and engineering quality control converted recurring low-frequency DAS responses into a common-frame thermal-slug trajectory library. For gas lift surveillance, operating-state DTS traces were combined with a dimensionless dual-band DAS coincidence field and reviewed with completion geometry, surface measurements, and event history. The workflows derive interpretive confidence from recurrence across events and concurrence across measurements, respectively. The results establish the feasibility of locating governed software implementation near domain expertise. Individual engineers and small technical teams can thereby retain tested methods within a shared technical foundation, shortening the cycle from field observation to reproducible operational workflow from many months to a few days.

title: Knowledge Organization Matters: How Graph Design and Temporal Structure Shape Agentic AI Performance on Drilling Activity Reports
abstract: Agentic AI over drilling reports can automate analytics that today take hours per question, from non-productive-time trending to offset-well lookup. Published systems typically commit to a single graph design without testing it: most studies in literature perform multi-method comparisons and evaluate whole pipelines and do not evaluate individual design decisions. We compare five ways of organizing a corpus for an agent (a vectorless reasoning tree, an open-vocabulary graph, that graph with community post-processing, a domain-schema graph, and a fine-grained quantitative graph) against a shared flat-vector baseline, on two public corpora: 1,681 Daily Drilling Reports from Equinor's Volve field (North Sea, 1992–2016) and 1,888 Weekly Activity Reports from Shell Offshore operations in the Gulf of Mexico (BSEE eWell archive, 2022–2024). We benchmark a ReAct agent that runs the full matrix at four capability tiers: two successive frontier versions, a fast-tier cloud model, and an open-weights 26B model on a 16 GB consumer GPU. Under frontier agents the vectorless tree leads relevance on both corpora, while hybrid retrieval leads completeness against machine-verified answer keys, with the domain-schema hybrid the strongest graph configuration. A blinded pair-preserved scoring of all 1,080 frontier cells confirms the BSEE architecture effects: hybrid retrieval beats vector-only (+0.040, Holm-corrected p=0.0004), the schema step over the open-vocabulary control is the largest effect measured (+0.068), and community post-processing alone does not contribute anything. The architecture ranking reproduces at every capability tier, and the spread widens as the agent weakens. A bi-temporal fact table with a point-in-time query tool raises as-of accuracy to 1.00 on both corpora, correcting all nine static errors with no regressions (96 paired queries, exact McNemar p=0.004). A schema audit shows the cost of a hand-designed ontology: named storms present in 30 reports were invisible to schema-graph retrieval, producing confident false negatives that open-vocabulary and vector retrieval avoided.

title: Tech-Enabled Recruitment Architecture for the Digital Energy Workforce
abstract: Energy sector organizations face persistent speed, accuracy, and fairness challenges in recruiting digitally skilled professionals, placing them at a disadvantage against technology firms competing for the same talent pool. At nuclear power generation organizations, this challenge is compounded by workforce scale and heterogeneity: recruitment must simultaneously serve high-volume outage staffing, safety-critical license-gated roles, specialized engineering and maintenance functions, and a large managed-service contractor population, often within a single hiring cycle. This paper proposes the architecture and implementation roadmap for a tech-enabled recruitment platform designed to accelerate identification, assessment, and selection of digital and specialized talent at a UAE nuclear energy organization. The proposed platform comprises four integrated components: a natural language processing (NLP) pipeline for semantic skills extraction using domain-specific entity recognition trained on energy sector role taxonomies, including verification screening for regulatory-gated roles; adaptive technical assessments calibrated to demonstrated capability across architecture, cloud, data engineering, and AI/ML competency areas; a structured interview scoring model using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) attribution designed to make cross-evaluator inconsistencies detectable and auditable; and end-to-end workflow automation integrated with the organization's HRMS. Candidate data governance is designed around a privacy-by-design framework with consent management, data minimization, and a full audit trail. Industry-wide benchmarks indicate the scale of efficiency gain such platforms can plausibly deliver: recent survey data from SHRM and LinkedIn indicate that organizations using AI in recruiting report material time and workload reductions in screening and administrative tasks, while independent academic literature on explainable AI demonstrates that SHAP-based attribution is a validated method for detecting bias in automated hiring decisions. This paper uses these external benchmarks, together with the organization's recruitment volumes and role diversity, to establish anticipated outcome ranges and a proposed evaluation framework for the platform, rather than reporting outcomes from a completed deployment. The paper concludes that tech-enabled recruitment is a strategic operational capability for nuclear and broader energy organizations, and that designing governance transparency, including algorithmic explainability and candidate data rights, into the platform from the outset positions transparency as a talent attraction differentiator rather than a compliance cost.

title: End-To-End Petrophysical Operations with Agentic AI: A Horizontal Carbonate Reservoir Well Case Study from a Mature Onshore Field, Abu Dhabi
abstract: Petrophysical work follows a well from planning through drilling and into completion, and at each step it usually passes between different specialists, vendor software, and email threads. This paper describes an in-house agentic artificial-intelligence assistant that brings those steps together behind one interface driven by text and voice. The system was validated end to end on a horizontal development well, denoted Well A here for confidentiality, drilled through a heterogeneous carbonate reservoir in a mature onshore field in Abu Dhabi. The assistant runs a fleet of nine configuration-driven skills grouped into two co-equal suites. A planning suite covers a well-data registry, document compilation, logging-program generation, cement-bond evaluation, and a logging-activity dashboard. An operations suite covers a vendor-aware quick-look interpretation pipeline, a production-log checklist automator, a drilling-correspondence router, and an inbox-triage dashboard. The skills chain deterministically: the daily geosteering report is parsed automatically, and the picked subzone tops seed per-zone Archie parameters straight into the log computation. On the case-study well, the planning package was assembled in about five minutes against a typical half-day of manual effort. During drilling, the cycle from a raw real-time log email to a delivered evaluation deck fell from roughly ninety minutes to under four minutes on a cached, scheduled run; the cold-start cycle on a log arriving from the rig for the first time, which is the one that governs how quickly the steering team sees an answer, ran between five and ten minutes. Automated subzone tagging let porosity and saturation cutoffs track a lithology change across adjacent subzones within the same shift, which supported steering decisions. Cement-bond and production-log preparation were completed within the shift the source data arrived. Reliability came from deterministic engineering beneath the language model: the evaluated interval was assembled from separate logging runs across two contractors, and porosity was computed per sample through a two-tier cascade of density-neutron porosity with a sonic fallback. The pipeline output was checked against an independent computer-based interpretation built in commercial petrophysical software on the same well. The petrophysical result is reported as computed, with the well name, reservoir zonation, and depths withheld for confidentiality.

title: Cross-Basin Analog Well Identification by Zone-Level Log Fingerprinting and Manifold Embedding: A Case Study of Western Desert, Egypt vs. Colorado and North Dakota, USA
abstract: Analog reasoning underpins subsurface decision-making, yet analog selection is often subjective and constrained by basin-specific stratigraphic conventions and the inconsistent availability of interpreted petrophysical products. We present a scalable workflow that represents each well-formation interval as a compact log fingerprint computed from robust statistics of standard petrophysical measurements (gamma ray, bulk density, neutron porosity, deep resistivity, and optionally compressional slowness), augmented with engineered neutron-density overlay-separation metrics and systematic outlier flags. Fingerprints are standardized and analyzed by unsupervised similarity learning: a two-dimensional manifold embedding visualizes neighborhood structure, density-based clustering identifies coherent analog families within and across formations, and representative type wells are exported to support interpretability and geological validation. We apply the workflow to a library of 18,658 formation-interval fingerprints spanning Western Desert (Egypt), Colorado (USA), and North Dakota (USA). To quantify separability, we introduce insularity diagnostics based on k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) mixing and label predictability. Mean cross-source mixing is 0.025, indicating strong source-domain separation, whereas mean cross-formation mixing is 0.258 (median 0.067), consistent with partial overlaps between formations and the presence of formation subtypes. A cross-validated linear classifier predicts source with 0.902 accuracy and formation label (50 classes) with 0.810 accuracy, confirming that both basin and stratigraphic signals are encoded in the fingerprint space. Case studies show that formation-conditioned embeddings separate internally consistent subtypes (e.g., Abu Roash F) while flagging quality-control candidates such as probable mis-picked intervals and systematic log-unit inconsistencies. Subtypes are further used to define play delineation: for the Mississippian Kibbey Lime (M-KL) in North Dakota, unsupervised ZoneGroups project geographically into a hydrocarbon-charged fairway near the Nesson Anticline versus a water-bearing basin margin, and for Abu Roash F in Egypt, resistivity-differentiated types segregate into producing and non-producing domains. The resulting similarity map provides a reproducible basis for analog retrieval, subtype characterization, and data-quality screening, and can be extended to downstream tasks such as log reconstruction and cross-asset model transfer.

title: Lightweight Edge AI Agent for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Distributed Acoustic Sensing
abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) systems generate large volumes of spatiotemporal data that challenge conventional cloud-centric monitoring architectures. Transmitting continuous DAS telemetry for centralized analysis introduces bandwidth, latency, and operational constraints, particularly in remote energy infrastructure environments. This paper presents a lightweight unsupervised edge AI agent for real-time anomaly detection operating on DAS measurements and derived multi-domain feature streams. The proposed framework integrates anomaly scoring, spatiotemporal clustering, trajectory-coherence validation, event severity assessment, autonomous action generation, online memory adaptation, and safety-aware state management within a unified edge-deployable architecture. An agentic processing loop performs perception, anomaly evaluation, event validation, action selection, learning, and safety monitoring while maintaining bounded computational requirements suitable for continuous field deployment. Coherent anomaly events are identified using spatial and temporal consistency criteria, enabling suppression of isolated artifacts and transient noise while preserving operationally meaningful patterns. Detected events are transformed into compact event-centric payloads containing severity, temporal extent, spatial extent, and decision metadata, substantially reducing communication requirements relative to raw data transmission. The framework further incorporates operational trust mechanisms including signed agent manifests, execution-path control, runtime watchdog monitoring, and fail-safe operating modes to support secure and reliable deployment in industrial environments. The framework was evaluated using synthetic datasets and real DAS datasets from field applications, including injection monitoring and microseismic event detection. Results demonstrate effective detection and prioritization of coherent spatiotemporal events without requiring labeled training data. Event-centric reporting reduced communication requirements by 94.36% while processing 1500 DAS channels with a peak memory footprint of 4.83 MB and an average latency below 1 s. The measured performance supports real-time edge deployment without dedicated accelerator hardware. The proposed framework enables scalable, explainable, and communication-efficient DAS monitoring by bringing intelligent event detection, validation, and decision support directly to the network edge.

title: Deep Learning for Acoustic Seismic Inversion: A Physics-Guided Generative Adversarial Network Approach
abstract: Acoustic impedance provides a quantitative link between reflection seismic data and reservoir properties, but deterministic inversion normally requires an extracted wavelet and an initial low-frequency impedance model. Errors in either input propagate into the inverted volume. This paper presents a three-dimensional, semi-supervised generative adversarial workflow that does not require an externally extracted wavelet or a prescribed low-frequency impedance model. A U-Net generator maps three input volumes to absolute acoustic impedance: the full-stack amplitude volume, a denoised and resolution-enhanced derivative, and a relative geologic time volume. A three-dimensional residual discriminator imposes a learned prior on impedance statistics. A differentiable forward operator converts predicted impedance to synthetic amplitudes, and their mismatch with the observed seismic contributes to the generator loss. The operator uses a laterally varying wavelet estimated by a dedicated network trained on approximately 400,000 synthetic examples; its weights remain fixed during inversion training, so wavelet estimation is not a separate well-based preprocessing step. Well logs provide sparse supervision. The workflow was applied to the public Groningen field dataset, where the mobile Zechstein salt and embedded anhydrite stringers complicate construction of a horizon-based initial model. The model was developed using 16 wells and validated against 4 blind wells over a 2,670.5-km2 survey. It achieved a median blind-well correlation of 0.82, reproduced the large-scale impedance trend without a prescribed low-frequency model, and produced more laterally continuous intra-salt stringers than are visible in a published deterministic result. Because the processing and display parameters differ, the latter comparison is qualitative.

title: Rigless Pump-Through Stimulation: A Breakthrough Approach to Reviving Underperforming Infill Wells in Heterogeneous Reservoirs
abstract: The primary objective of this paper is to present a novel, cost-effective rigless stimulation methodology developed to rescue a major infill drilling program in a mature, highly heterogeneous glaciogenic sandstone reservoir in Southern Oman. The project faced severe economic threats when over 50 newly drilled wells exhibited Productivity Indices (PI) 40-60% lower than legacy wells due to drilling-induced formation damage. Conventional rig-based workover stimulation was economically unviable at this scale. This paper details the diagnostic-driven approach and the subsequent operational innovation - standalone "pump-through" technique - that successfully restored production while slashing intervention costs. A rigorous diagnostic workflow was implemented to identify the root causes of underperformance. Systematic skin analysis utilizing PI-theoretical versus PI-actual cross plots confirmed high induced skin. Kh versus PI categorization isolated inflow-restricted wells as prime candidates. Crucially, QEMSCAN mineralogy assessments revealed significant heterogeneity in clay content (Illite/Kaolinite), dictating the need for tailored acid systems rather than a uniform approach. To execute the stimulation economically, a first of its kind rigless operational method was engineered. Instead of mobilizing a workover rig to pull the artificial lift system, a standalone pump was connected directly to the annulus at the surface. The downhole traveling valve of the existing beam pump was specially configured to prevent acid backflow into the tubing, protecting the artificial lift integrity. A five-campaign systematic trial was conducted to optimize the treatment recipe, evolving from fixed volume 10% HCl to capacity-based sizing with 15% HCl, solvent pre-flushes for heavy oil, and HF-blends for silica-rich flank zones. The tailored, rigless stimulation strategy yielded exceptional results, fundamentally altering the project's economic trajectory. The operational innovation of pumping through the annulus with the beam pump in place achieved a ~60% reduction in intervention costs per well by eliminating rig mobilization. Furthermore, production deferment was minimized from several days to mere hours, and the risk of further formation damage from kill fluids was entirely mitigated. Production results improved dramatically through the five optimization campaigns. While initial trials yielded a 52% gross production increase, the fully optimized recipe (Campaign 3 and 4) delivered up to a 400% gross increase, immediately exceeding forecasted oil rates. The data-driven approach proved that uniform stimulation is suboptimal in heterogeneous reservoirs, and that integrating advanced diagnostics with operational innovation can successfully revive marginal or damaged wells. This paper introduces a pioneering "standalone bullhead" stimulation technique that maintains artificial lift integrity during acid injection. By combining this operational breakthrough with a highly tailored, mineralogy-driven chemical strategy, the study provides a scalable, field-tested blueprint for operators seeking to maximize recovery and minimize costs in mature, heterogeneous fields facing widespread formation damage.

title: Chemical Water Shut-Off Bullhead Treatment in ICD-Completed Horizontal Well: Design, Simulation, and Field Results
abstract: This paper details the design and successful field application of a chemical water shut off (CWSO) treatment in a horizontal oil well completed with inflow control devices (ICDs). The case study is from an onshore UAE oilfield producing from a carbonate/dolomite reservoir characterized by the presence of high conductive features like fractures, high-permeability streaks and karst. The reservoir is supported by a strong aquifer, which has led to water channeling and high field water cuts (exceeding 60%). Although the combined application of microgel + gel by bull-heading injection has proven effective in other open-hole wells within similar carbonate reservoirs, its implementation in ICD equipped completions is unprecedent. One of the main challenges was ensuring the gelant formulation retains gelling properties after passing through ICD nozzles under high shear conditions. This paper outlines the treatment design—based on laboratory and simulation studies—and field results. Laboratory shearing tests, using the GelixTM formulation, evaluated the impact of shear rate on gel properties by injecting it through a capillary at increasing flow rates. Reservoir simulations aimed to: (i) forecast post-treatment production, (ii) optimize injected volume via sensitivity analysis, and (iii) compare results with mechanical water shut-off by isolation of the highest water-producing interval. Once designed, the chemical WSO treatment was injected into the well in the bullhead mode. PLTs were performed before and after the treatment to assess the placement of the gel. Production data before and after treatment were compared to evaluate the impact on production performance. Laboratory results confirmed that the gelling properties remained unchanged under high shear flow, indicating ICDs would not impair gelling in the reservoir. Simulation study validated the initial 200 m3 treatment volume, with sensitivity tests showing 200-250 m3 of gel yielded optimal incremental oil production. Two years post-treatment, incremental oil production was estimated at 36,000-49,000 bbl. While long-term results for CWSO and mechanical shut-off were similar, CWSO provided a significant short-term oil production peak followed by a slower decline than before the treatment. At last, field application resulted in a reduction of water cut from 91% to 85% matching simulation predictions. Post-treatment PLT confirmed the reduction of water inflow from the highest contributing ICD stage, while well liquid productivity dropped from 32 to 11.8 stb/d/psi. These results confirmed that the treatment effectively targeted the main water-producing zone and that ICDs did not compromise gel performance. It is the first field in Abu Dhabi to implement microgel/gel/microgel technology for water shut off. It is also the first time that this technology is injected in bullhead mode through ICDs equipped horizontal well. This field case study demonstrates that the technology is effective for horizontal wells equipped with ICD's completions as proven before in open hole completions.

title: Corrosivity Evaluation and Corrosion Mechanism Assessment of Unpiggable Flowline Networks in Mature Upstream Systems
abstract: This paper presents a laboratory- and field-validated, mechanism-based assessment of corrosion associated with recurring loss of primary containment (LOPC) events in un-piggable multiphase flowline systems. The study investigates the principal degradation mechanisms contributing to repeated leaks through an integrated assessment of historical operating conditions, produced-fluid chemistry, reservoir characteristics, corrosion morphology, metallurgical condition, topographical effects, laboratory corrosivity, and integrity management practices. Historical leak records to establish correlations between observed degradation and operating conditions and to support the development of targeted mitigation and integrity management measures. Unlike conventional corrosion assessment approaches, this study adopts a multidisciplinary framework that integrates historical and current datasets into a unified analysis methodology. The assessment considered design and operating parameters, including temperature, flow velocity, and flow regime, together with reservoir characteristics and CO2 and H2S concentrations. Corrosion monitoring data, laboratory corrosivity and corrosion inhibitor testing, microbiological assessments, metallurgical investigations, and GIS-based topographical evaluations were incorporated into the analysis. Representative cut sections from failed flowlines were examined to characterize corrosion morphology and establish consistency between field observations and laboratory findings. The resulting datasets were correlated with historical leak trends and inspection results to identify the principal factors associated with failure. The assessment identified internal CO2 corrosion as the dominant degradation mechanism and the principal contributor to recurring LOPC events within the evaluated surface-laid, un-piggable flowline network. Metallurgical examination, corrosion morphology, laboratory testing, and microbiological assessments did not provide conclusive evidence that alternative mechanisms, including microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC), were the primary cause of failure. Corrosion severity was strongly associated with increasing water cut, elevated operating temperature, CO2-rich production fluids, low flow velocity, topographical conditions conducive to liquid accumulation, and the transition from natural flow to gas-lift operation. These conditions increased the potential for CO2 dissolution, localized acidification, disruption of protective iron carbonate (FeCO3) films, and localized flow-assisted corrosion. The absence of continuous corrosion inhibition and operational pigging, together with inadequate mothballing practices for inactive flowlines, further contributed to localized pitting and under-deposit corrosion under multiphase-flow conditions. In-situ pH modelling and scale-tendency assessments identified corrosive stagnant zones consistent with the observed pit morphology and leak locations. Historical leak analysis also showed that failures occurred substantially earlier than the anticipated design life, indicating a discrepancy between assumed corrosion allowances and actual degradation rates. Although optimized corrosion inhibitor programs improved mitigation performance, the findings demonstrate that chemical treatment alone cannot provide a sufficient standalone integrity barrier. Effective corrosion management in mature brownfield systems therefore requires an integrated, mechanism-based approach combining laboratory validation, inspection feedback, operational optimization, appropriate pigging strategies, and strengthened corrosion governance. Such an approach provides a more robust basis for distinguishing competing degradation mechanisms, prioritizing integrity risks, and selecting fit-for-purpose mitigation measures, thereby improving flowline reliability and reducing the likelihood of future LOPC events. This integrated approach enables improved differentiation of competing corrosion mechanisms and strengthens corrosion mitigation strategies, integrity management practices, and decision-making, thereby enhancing pipeline reliability, improving process safety, and reducing loss of primary containment (LOPC) events.

title: Trajectory-Aware Drilling Risk Scoring: An Agentic LLM Approach to Offset Well Selection and Dynamic Section Risk Assessment
abstract: Well planning today relies on manual offset well selection and labelled NPT events, systematically missing trajectory-related risks that affect drilling performance even if the operations are not halted completely but overall performance is affected. This paper presents an AI-powered system that automatically identifies relevant offset wells, extracts trajectory-driven drilling risks from Daily Drilling Reports, and generates an explainable, dynamic section risk score for planned wells, enabling engineers to quantify and compare the risk implications of trajectory design decisions before spud. A customized LLM pipeline agent processes DDR narratives and directional survey data from offset wells. A trajectory similarity index, built on trajectory/geometry feature like KOP depth, inclination, dogleg severity, tortuosity, TVD/MD ratio, and spatial proximity; automatically selects the most comparable offset well sections as reference set using a similarity scoring algorithm. In parallel, an LLM agent extracts and classifies incidents from those offset wells into trajectory-related risk categories, capturing both formally labelled NPT and hidden risks such as tight hole, overpull, and steerability challenges. SME-assigned weights across trajectory control, BHA performance, hole cleaning, and ROP efficiency produce a 0–100 section risk score, propagated through similarity-weighted averaging and automatically updated whenever the planned trajectory is modified. The system successfully extracted and quantified section-level trajectory risks from structured DDR narratives, demonstrating that incident evidence can be systematically recovered and compared across offset well sections minimizing manual review in minutes rather than days. When engineers modify the trajectory by changing KOP depth, build rate, or maximum inclination of the planned well, the system immediately recalculates the similarity index with the offset wells that had the highest level of similarity now that the trajectory changed to match those wells that are most similar in terms of the trajectory as some of the parameters for similarity, refreshes the reference set of offset wells pool, and updates section risk scores, providing an instant view of how each trajectory decision shifts the risk profile relative to historical offset performance. LLM-based extraction recovered trajectory-related incidents of labeled NPT incidents and no NPT labeled events, including steerability issues, excessive drag, torque showing that a significant chunk of hidden incidents are not initially labeled, sometimes up to by 50% compared to labelled NPT alone for iterations run within Volve field; which shows there is a high percentage of incidents that are not reported and flagged initially as NPT, which is the flag used conventionally by engineers to filter data from SQL queries. The tool enables engineers to identify which offset well sections are most geometrically similar to the planned well that can be used on top of closest wells by distance and surface after being narrowed down and therefore carry the most relevant risk evidence, making the comparison objective, repeatable, and directly tied to trajectory geometry rather than engineer judgement. The entire workflow is orchestrated by the LLM, significantly reducing the time required to assess design changes and ensuring that every trajectory modification is immediately reflected in an updated, evidence-backed risk score. While recent agentic-LLM approaches have advanced drilling-risk analysis, they stop short of a trajectory-linked, dynamic risk score. Chica et al. (2025) [1] extract hidden, non-NPT-labeled risk from DDR text but do not connect that risk to well geometry or offset selection, and produce no section-level score. Spagnolo et al. (2026) [2] fuse structured and unstructured drilling data for retrieval and insight but likewise generate neither a similarity-ranked offset set nor a quantified risk value. Prior similarity-based offset methods [5, 6] rank analogues on well features but do not read narrative text for hidden risk, and prior NPT/DDR-extraction methods recover risk signal from text but do not tie it to trajectory geometry or recompute as the plan changes. The novelty of this work is therefore not any single component but their integration into one closed loop: trajectory-geometry similarity selects the offset set, an LLM recovers both labeled and hidden risk from those offsets' DDRs, and a deterministic engine converts that evidence into a section-level score that is automatically re-derived whenever the planned trajectory is edited. Unlike prior agentic-LLM drilling workflows, which either extract hidden risk from text or rank offsets by well features but never link the two, this system makes the section risk score a live function of trajectory geometry: editing the plan re-selects offsets and re-blends their extracted risk automatically. By orchestrating the full workflow through an LLM agent, the system eliminates manual bottlenecks and delivers immediate risk score updates as trajectory designs evolve representing a meaningful advance in proactive, data-driven well planning.

title: Stratigraphy-Guided Physics-Informed Semi-Supervised CNN–Transformer for Acoustic Impedance and Resistivity Inversion
abstract: Accurate reservoir characterization remains challenging due to complex geological heterogeneity, limited well control, and uncertain seismic-property relationships. This study presents a stratigraphy-guided physics-informed semi-supervised CNN-Transformer framework for joint acoustic impedance (AI) and resistivity (RT) inversion in carbonate reservoirs. The proposed framework integrates post-stack seismic data, well-log measurements, and interpreted stratigraphic horizons within a unified deep learning framework. A differentiable seismic forward modeling module is incorporated to establish a physics-informed constraint between predicted AI and observed seismic responses, enabling unlabeled seismic data to participate in model optimization. Stratigraphic horizons are embedded as geological encoding information during network learning rather than used as post-processing corrections, allowing geological knowledge to improve reservoir boundary preservation and spatial continuity. Furthermore, joint AI-RT inversion integrates elastic and electrical responses to provide complementary information for reservoir characterization and fluid discrimination. The proposed framework is applied to a carbonate reservoir dataset containing 3D seismic data, well logs, and stratigraphic interpretations. Blind-well validation is performed to evaluate the prediction capability of AI and RT under limited well supervision. The results demonstrate improved seismic consistency, geological continuity, and reservoir characterization capability compared with purely data-driven inversion approaches. The integrated AI-RT interpretation provides additional insights for identifying favorable hydrocarbon-bearing intervals and reducing reservoir characterization uncertainty. This study demonstrates that combining seismic physics, geological constraints, and deep learning provides an effective framework for multi-property reservoir characterization in complex carbonate reservoirs and supports exploration and development decision-making.

title: Integrated Seismic Inversion and Multi-Attribute Analysis for Carbonate Porosity Delineation: A Case Study from Rajasthan Basin
abstract: Although clastic reservoirs constitute approximately 70% of petroleum reservoirs worldwide, carbonate reservoirs contain more than 60% of the world's proven oil reserves and play a significant role in global hydrocarbon production (Qi and Liu 2024). Carbonate reservoirs are inherently complex due to heterogeneous lithology; pore systems are more complex in carbonate rocks than they are in clastics. While clastic rocks have mainly intergranular pores, carbonate rocks can have a variety of pore types, such as moldic, vuggy, interparticle, and intraparticle. Accurate prediction of porosity is critical for effective reservoir characterization in carbonates, however, seismic responses in carbonate rocks are poorly understood. In addition, DHI ranking and AVO classification systems developed for clastic rocks are unlikely to be applicable to carbonate rocks. The study area, located in the western part of the Bikaner–Nagaur Sub-Basin of Rajasthan, hosts heavy oil (API 8-10°) within the Neoproterozoic Carbonate Formation. In this study, a post-stack model-based seismic inversion workflow was implemented to generate a high-resolution P-impedance (Zp) volume by integrating 3D seismic data with well log information. The inverted P-impedance volume was further utilized in a multi-attribute regression framework to predict neutron porosity across the target interval. Neutron porosity is chosen as the primary petrophysical target because the neutron log responds predominantly to hydrogen contained within pore fluids and therefore provides an estimate of fluid-filled formation porosity. In carbonate reservoirs characterized by fracture and vug development, neutron-derived porosity is commonly integrated with other logs for reservoir characterization and serves as a suitable target property for seismic inversion and multi-attribute porosity prediction. In the absence of core-calibrated effective or total porosity logs, neutron porosity was adopted as the target reservoir property for this study. The neutron log, typically calibrated on a limestone matrix, provides a reasonable representation of porosity in carbonate formations and is therefore considered appropriate for the present reservoir. The inverted impedance result reveals clear lithological differentiation within the carbonate formation, with the upper interval dominated by massive dolomitic carbonates and the lower interval characterized by interbedded clastic sequences (sand–shale) interspersed with carbonate streaks. The analysis indicates that the lower clastic unit exhibits relatively lower impedance and higher porosity whereas the upper unit of the formation is associated with relatively high impedance values and relatively low porosity and additionally, localized zones of elevated porosity and low impedance within the upper unit combinedly suggest the presence of secondary and tertiary porosities as inferred from the borehole image log. The predicted neutron porosity volume shows strong agreement with blind wells data and demonstrates consistency with the inverted impedance trends, confirming the reliability of the integrated workflow. The study provides very good porosity distribution within the carbonate and offers valuable inputs for reservoir characterization, static modelling, and future field development planning.

title: Evaluating AI for Speed, Consistency, and Traceability in Energy Regulatory Decision Support
abstract: This paper evaluates select Artificial Intelligence (AI) setups designed to audit anonymised safety case submissions of petroleum operators for regulatory compliance. We compared a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Pipeline (using gpt-4o-mini) against a One-Shot Baseline (direct gpt-4o-mini processing) and an Agentic AI (using gemini-2.5-flash, and Antigravity as harness). We demonstrated that automated reviews achieve notable speedups over manual reviews, up to 240.8x for RAG and 634.8x for the Agentic AI. While the One-Shot Baseline is the fastest overall (2 to 6 minutes), RAG and the Agentic AI showed higher recall in discovering compliance omissions on large documents (e.g., the 564-page SUB-002). We also identified a self-evaluation bias, where gpt-4o-mini rates its own faithfulness much higher (4.13/5.0) than the judge (2.21/5.0).

title: A Case Study on Design Strategies and Overcoming Challenges in a 100.8 MW Wind Energy Project in India
abstract: This paper discusses the development of a 100.8 MW captive onshore wind project designed to supply renewable electricity to refinery operations in western and central India. The case study follows the project from early site screening to commissioning readiness, with attention to the engineering decisions that shaped wind measurement, layout planning, foundation design, logistics, grid connection and construction sequencing. Rather than presenting the project only as a feasibility exercise, the paper focuses on how the design was adapted to real site conditions, including land availability, road access, monsoon constraints, utility interfaces, local coordination and execution risk. The project is also examined as part of industrial decarbonization, where large energy consumers need renewable power that is technically reliable, commercially viable and practical to deliver on the ground. The project was developed through an integrated review of wind resource, land suitability, grid access, constructability, regulatory requirements and local sensitivities. Wind conditions were studied using 120 m meteorological masts, long-term correlation and energy-yield modelling. Turbine locations were then refined in WindPRO to manage wake losses while still allowing practical road access, cable routing, crane movement, environmental buffers and safe erection. Foundation designs were prepared using turbine-wise geotechnical findings rather than applying one uniform design across all locations. Logistics planning included route surveys, strengthening checks and movement strategies for long blades and other oversized components. Electrical planning covered pooling substations, transformers, protection systems, SCADA, forecasting, scheduling and coordination with the utility network. The project is expected to deliver a capacity utilization factor of about 32-34%, with annual generation in the range of 280-310 GWh. Layout optimization kept modelled wake losses within about 5-8%, while internal electrical and evacuation losses were treated separately in the energy estimate. The project is expected to avoid about 290,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year. The main observation from the case is that a captive wind project of this scale cannot be managed through sequential engineering alone. Wind assessment, layout design, foundation engineering, transport planning, grid-interface work and stakeholder engagement have to progress together. Early route checks, reserve micrositing options, monsoon-aware planning and interim evacuation arrangements helped reduce execution risk and protected the overall project schedule. The paper contributes practical insight into how a captive wind project can be structured for an energy intensive industrial consumer. In this type of project, generation performance, grid access, land control, power quality and commercial deliverability have to be solved as one connected problem. The case shows that moderate-wind sites can still support a bankable development when turbine configuration, hub height, micrositing, wake-loss control, foundation design, transport feasibility, reactive power support and evacuation planning are aligned early. The experience is relevant for developers, industrial consumers, EPC contractors, utilities, lenders, consultants and policy practitioners working in markets where land, access, grid capacity, open-access charges and local coordination can influence project success as much as the wind resource itself.

title: Strategy and Crisis Monitor: An AI-Enabled Autonomous Maritime Monitor for Disruption Intelligence and Operational Resilience
abstract: This paper presents the Strategy and Crisis Monitor, an agentic artificial-intelligence (AI) enabled executive dashboard conceived, built, and deployed end-to-end in days to track regional events, incidents, transport disruption, and energy-market signals during a live crisis. The work pursues three objectives: to demonstrate that autonomous AI agents can convert public maritime, energy, and trade data into always-on disruption intelligence; to replace the analyst-curated executive briefing with a live, evidence-linked signal layer operating under human oversight; and to compress executive decision latency from days to minutes. The architecture comprises three operational layers. An ingestion layer of autonomous agents continuously normalizes heterogeneous public sources, including multilateral chokepoint transit data, vessel-tracking feeds derived from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), international oil and gas statistics, and maritime trade and connectivity indicators, supplemented by market context as evidence layers. A classification layer maps incoming data against a rules-based event taxonomy covering chokepoint disruption, export-route stress, gas exposure, port-connectivity deterioration, and regional trade impact. A prioritization layer scores signals using a weighted composite risk index with exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and cumulative sum (CUSUM) anomaly detection, and surfaces them through a 60-second executive scan pattern with full drill-down to underlying sources. Deployed live during the March 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption, when average daily transits collapsed by approximately 95% against the February baseline and the benchmark very large crude carrier (VLCC) rate reached an all-time high, the platform was used to brief senior leadership of a major national maritime and energy logistics operator in near real time. It reduced executive decision latency from a typical 24- to 72-hour analyst cycle to under five minutes per signal, a compression factor of roughly 290 to 860, while integrating more than 40 public indicators. The same detection logic was subsequently applied retrospectively to four historical chokepoint crises, in the Red Sea (2023 to 2024), the Suez Canal (2021), the Strait of Hormuz (2019), and the Panama Canal (2023 to 2024), confirming that the monitored public signals were available weeks to months ahead of official statistics in every case. Those case studies were reconstructed with knowledge of how each episode unfolded and therefore document signal availability and design generality rather than prospective detection performance. The contribution is twofold and is, to the authors’ knowledge, the first implementation of its kind in the maritime-resilience and energy-logistics literature. First, a decision-method contribution: passive public reporting feeds are converted into a structured, always-on resilience instrument fusing maritime, energy, and trade signals in a single operating view. Second, an operating-model contribution: the architecture is public-data-native, lightweight to sustain, and reproducible across operating companies, corridors, and risk domains, and is presented together with the governance, oversight, and control mechanisms required before agentic AI is admitted to a critical operational environment. Both are directly actionable for practicing engineers and planners in operations, strategy, and resilience roles.

title: Real-Time Operator Fatigue Detection Using Physics-Informed AI and Standard Camera Infrastructure
abstract: This paper presents a real-time physiological fatigue monitoring system for energy facility operators using standard camera hardware. The system applies remote photoplethysmography to extract heart rate and heart rate variability from facial video without wearable sensors. It targets control room personnel, drilling supervisors, and offshore operators. A key objective is equitable detection performance across all skin tones present in multinational energy workforces. A seven-stage Physics-Informed Synthetic Dataset generation pipeline (PISD-rPPG) was developed. Photorealistic operator faces were generated using StyleGAN3 and animated using SadTalker. Physiological signals were synthesized with NeuroKit2 and refined using a diffusion model. Forward Plane-Orthogonal-to-Skin (POS) validation confirmed signal integrity before reverse-POS embedding injected signals at melanin-dependent amplitudes derived from Beer-Lambert absorption physics, producing skin-tone-accurate training data across all six Fitzpatrick classifications. A Temporal Shift Convolutional Attention Network (TSCAN) was pre-trained on the synthetic dataset and evaluated on subjects from the MMPD dataset that were unseen during training. The prototype targets a capture rate of 30 Hz and scores operator fatigue using three personalized physiological thresholds calibrated against individual baselines. The study employed a controlled comparison protocol. TSCAN was pre-trained on 793 synthetic videos generated through the PISD-rPPG pipeline and evaluated against the full MMPD real-world dataset as a cross-domain transfer test, achieving a mean absolute error of 15.7 BPM. This result confirms that physics-informed synthetic data produces signal representations that transfer to real camera footage without any exposure to real training subjects. Under the same protocol, an unrefined physics-based baseline of 80 synthetic videos reached 17.2 BPM. The published SCAMPS reference of 2,800 synthetic videos (McDuff et al., 2022) reports 19.05 BPM under a separately published test configuration. Because dataset size and refinement differ together, that gap is reported as a combined effect and not as the contribution of the diffusion stage alone. Demographic fairness across Fitzpatrick Types III-IV and Types V-VI is an objective of the pipeline design rather than a result of this study, and no per-group figures are claimed, since that evaluation is still under replication. The prototype classifies operator fatigue into three graded states: Normal, Mild Fatigue, and Severe Fatigue, each triggering a corresponding supervisor alert. Status descriptions are generated by a rule-based condition engine requiring no language model. Face detection and cropping occur on the operator device, and no full-frame video is transmitted or stored. No hardware beyond existing facility cameras is required. This paper presents the first application of a physics-informed synthetic training strategy for rPPG-based operator fatigue monitoring in energy facilities. The synthetic pre-training stage addresses demographic bias without requiring real subject data, while the diffusion refinement stage demonstrates that effective domain adaptation requires no real subjects at all. This combination is directly relevant to energy industry deployment contexts where diverse workforces and limited data collection opportunities are practical constraints. One boundary should be read carefully. The accuracy reported here is for heart-rate estimation on benchmark data. Fatigue detection itself has not been validated against a fatigue reference in any operator, and a controlled operator pilot is the next stage of this work.

title: Operational Risks and AI Bias in LLM-Based Agentic Systems for a Process Plant: Electric Motor Operations Case Study (Oil & Gas)
abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has encouraged many industries to explore Agentic AI. Earlier AI tools were used mainly for data analysis and information retrieval. Newer systems can carry out a sequence of related tasks, combine information from several engineering sources and prepare recommendations with relatively limited user input. These capabilities can support document review, procurement quality, maintenance planning, commissioning and operational troubleshooting. However, they also bring risks that are not normally associated with conventional engineering software. Because the output is probabilistic, a recommendation may be influenced by missing technical information, incomplete operating context, biased source material or incorrect interpretation of safety-critical requirements. It may still appear convincing even when its engineering basis is weak. Electric motors are used throughout oil and gas facilities and are essential to the operation of pumps, compressors, fans, cooling systems and other plant equipment. A motor failure can interrupt production and, in some cases, affect the safety or reliability of the wider process. Decisions relating to motor protection, alarms, equipment condition, commissioning, fault diagnosis and maintenance therefore require sound engineering judgement, supported by approved protection settings, operating history, OEM guidance and relevant international standards. This makes electric motors a practical case for examining the use of LLM-based Agentic AI in a safety-critical engineering environment. The paper considers a series of representative motor scenarios covering design review, Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), commissioning, operational troubleshooting, predictive maintenance, alarm assessment and root cause analysis. The findings show that prediction accuracy and model confidence alone do not establish whether an AI recommendation is safe or technically reliable. That judgement depends on the quality of the available evidence, the completeness of the operating context, compliance with applicable standards and protection philosophy, and verification by a qualified engineer. To manage these risks, the paper introduces the Engineering Trustworthiness Assurance Framework (ETAF). It brings the main checks into one process, starting with the quality of the available engineering information and ending with the approval of the final recommendation. ETAF includes the Engineering AI Assurance Pyramid (EAAP), the Operational AI Risk Propagation Model (OARPM) and the AI Engineering Governance Matrix (AEGM). It also uses three assessment measures: the Engineering Trustworthiness Score (ETS), AI Recommendation Criticality Level (ARCL) and Engineering Confidence Index (ECI). These are proposed as practical, illustrative tools that organisations can adapt when introducing LLM-assisted decision support in safety-critical engineering work. Although the representative scenarios are based on electric motor operations, the proposed framework is applicable to other classes of rotating equipment deployed throughout upstream, midstream, and downstream oil and gas facilities. The paper contributes a practical engineering governance approach that complements existing AI assurance initiatives by emphasizing engineering trustworthiness, protection philosophy, operational accountability, and responsible human oversight during the deployment of Agentic AI systems.

title: Decoding Residual Oil (RZO), Mobile Oil and Solid Bitumen: An Integrated Geochemical Methodology for Characterizing Hydrocarbons Near or Below the Oil Water Contact (OWC) and Free Water Level (FWL)
abstract: Carbonate reservoirs commonly contain hydrocarbon accumulations below the interpreted free water level (FWL) and oil-water contact (OWC), creating significant uncertainty regarding hydrocarbon saturation, fluid mobility, reserves estimation, and development strategy. Conventional petrophysical evaluation often identifies these intervals as hydrocarbon-bearing; however, production performance may be poor if the retained hydrocarbons occur predominantly as immobile residual oil or solid bitumen. This study presents an integrated geochemical and petrographic workflow to characterize hydrocarbon occurrence, mobility, alteration, and charge history within a giant carbonate reservoir in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The workflow combines mud-log gas evaluation using Total Gas and Wetness-Balance ratios, solvent extraction and extract-yield measurements, Rock-Eval pyrolysis (S1, S2, and pyrogram characterization), Saturate-Aromatic-Resin-Asphaltene (SARA) analysis, gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS), Low-Temperature Hydrous Pyrolysis (LTHP), and petrographic and SEM-EDX investigations. These complementary datasets were integrated with petrophysical observations to understand hydrocarbon presence, distinguish mobile hydrocarbons from residual oil and solid bitumen and to evaluate their distribution relative to the FWL and OWC. The study also assessed the role of biodegradation, charge mixing, and structural evolution in controlling present-day fluid distribution. The results demonstrate that hydrocarbons occurring below the FWL comprise varying proportions of mobile oil, residual extractable oil, and pervasive pore-filling solid bitumen. Extract-yield and pyrolysis data reveal a systematic decline in hydrocarbon mobility from crestal locations toward flank positions and below fluid contacts. Samples associated with productive oil columns exhibit elevated Total Gas, extract yield, S1 yield, and saturate content, whereas intervals dominated by residual hydrocarbons are characterized by lower gas readings, reduced S1 yields, higher S2 yields, and enrichment in resin and asphaltene fractions. GC-MS chromatograms reveal a spectrum of oil alteration, ranging from relatively fresh oils with smooth baselines and complete n-alkane envelopes to heavily altered hydrocarbons characterized by prominent UCM humps and pronounced n-alkane depletion. The coexistence of a substantial UCM hump together with preserved n-alkanes in many samples indicates that biodegradation was followed by a subsequent hydrocarbon charging event, resulting in mixing between an earlier degraded paleo-oil and a later, more mature oil charge. Petrographic observations and SEM-EDX analyses confirm that solid bitumen occupies approximately 21–37% of pore space in selected samples, reducing pore connectivity and contributing to hydrocarbon immobility. LTHP further demonstrates that total hydrocarbon saturation can substantially exceed the fraction that is mobile under primary depletion conditions. Although mobile oil volumes are generally limited, a significant proportion of hydrocarbons remains potentially recoverable through enhanced oil recovery (EOR) processes. Collectively, the integrated dataset indicates that hydrocarbons below the FWL represent a complex mixture of biodegraded paleo-oil, residual extractable oil, and solid bitumen preserved through multiple charging, alteration, and remigration events associated with the tectonic evolution of the field. CSIA results further contextualize these mobility and alteration patterns within the broader framework of reservoir connectivity. The limited carbon-isotope variability observed among MDT oils, produced oils, and crestal-to-flank core extracts indicates a common source and comparable maturity level. This CSIA-based interpretation is important for field-scale reservoir modelling, as it supports a laterally connected petroleum system while acknowledging significant spatial heterogeneity in oil quality and producibility. This study demonstrates that integrating mud-gas interpretation, extract yield, pyrolysis, SARA, GC-MS, LTHP, CSIA, and petrographic techniques provides a robust methodology for differentiating mobile and immobile hydrocarbons in carbonate reservoirs. The workflow improves estimation of recoverable resources, reduces uncertainty in reserves evaluation, and supports the selection of appropriate development and EOR strategies in reservoirs containing significant residual oil and solid bitumen accumulations.

title: Scaling Subsurface Interpretation with Seismic Foundation Models and Agentic Workflows
abstract: Seismic interpretation is rarely a single-task exercise. In practice, an interpreter moves back and forth between data quality, reflector continuity, fault expression, stratigraphic organization, seismic attributes, well control, and geological judgment. A fault cube, a horizon volume, or a conditioned seismic section may each be useful on its own, but none of them is sufficient if the outputs are disconnected from the rest of the interpretation workflow. This paper presents SeismicGen, a framework developed to make seismic AI more reusable and more consistent across interpretation tasks. The workflow is built around a Seismic Foundation Model, or SFM, that provides a shared seismic representation for several specialized interpretation agents. These agents support seismic conditioning, fault characterization, relative geological time estimation, relative acoustic impedance generation, fault and horizon extraction, seismic-to-well tie, and geobody detection. The purpose is not to replace the interpreter with a black-box system, but to provide a common technical layer that helps different AI outputs remain consistent with one another. The workflow starts with seismic preparation, normalization, and quality control. Depending on the interpretation objective, the seismic volume is then passed through selected agents. The outputs are not treated as isolated products. For example, fault probability and displacement indicators can guide fault-surface extraction, while relative geological time can support horizon organization. Results are checked through section-by-section review, geological consistency checks, residual and amplitude analysis, comparison with available well information, and interpreter-led validation. The main practical issue addressed in this paper is the lack of continuity between many existing seismic AI tools. A model may detect faults or pick horizons, but the output often remains separate from the broader interpretation process. SeismicGen is designed to connect these tasks through one shared representation and a coordinated agent workflow. Initial applications indicate that this structure can reduce repetitive interpretation effort, improve consistency between interpretation products, and shorten the path from seismic volume to review-ready subsurface outputs. The contribution of the paper is a practical architecture for applying foundation-model and agentic-AI concepts to seismic interpretation. The paper focuses on workflow design, technical integration, quality control, and interpreter validation, without requiring disclosure of proprietary model architecture.

authors.name: H. Mustapha

title: Proppant Pack Conductivity Under Closure Stress: Physically Bounded Permeability Model
abstract: Reservoir stimulation enables production from low permeability reservoirs by creating hydraulic fractures that serve as flow pathways between the formation and the wellbore. Proppants keep these fractures open against the closure stress of the formation, and the conductivity of the proppant pack is critical for well deliverability throughout the life of the field. In the industry, engineers estimate the decay of proppant permeability using exponential decay functions, but these functions carry a fundamental defect: they predict both zero porosity and zero permeability as the effective closure stress increases, with no physically bounded lower limit. This study proposes new asymptotically correct relations between proppant permeability and applied stress that serve as potential substitutes for the conventional exponential decay models. The work reformulates three established compressibility models (hyperbolic, exponential, and power) in terms of the yield stress, computed at the point of maximum curvature of the compression curve consistent with the Casagrande method, and derives permeability models with bounded asymptotes through the power relation between permeability and void ratio. We compare the predictions of the proposed models with proppant and sand data compiled from published studies, and evaluate performance against the conventional exponential model. The hyperbolic model fits the compression data best, including the sharp decrease in void ratio after yield in brittle sands. The proposed permeability models predict the hydraulic conductivity from the fitted compressibility parameters with a single free λ-exponent, while the conventional model underpredicts or overpredicts the conductivity around the yield stress and the difference grows at high stress where the pack retains a finite residual conductivity. The framework implements in three stages: characterize the proppant once through standard laboratory tests, predict the permeability at any effective closure stress, and integrate the revised equations into fracture models for production forecasting in unconventional and geothermal operations.

title: Generation of a New Empirical IPR Correlation for Vertical Wells Producing from Multi-Layered Oil Reservoirs with Crossflow Between the Layers
abstract: The Inflow Performance Relationship (IPR) is a foundational tool in petroleum production engineering, quantifying the relationship between reservoir pressure drawdown and wellbore oil production rate. Classical empirical IPR correlations, most notably Vogel (1968), Klins and Majcher (1992), and Wiggins (1994)—were derived for single-layer, solution-gas-drive reservoirs through numerical simulation and regression analysis. Despite their widespread adoption over more than five decades, these correlations share a critical and well-documented limitation: none accounts for the inter-layer crossflow that occurs in multilayer reservoirs where adjacent layers communicate under contrasting pressure conditions. In multilayer systems with active crossflow, a low-pressure layer can act as a net fluid receiver rather than a producer, exhibiting negative production rates at high bottomhole pressures—a physical regime entirely outside the predictive scope of all existing empirical correlations. This study fills that gap by developing and validating the first closed-form, dimensionless empirical IPR correlation for vertical wells completed across two communicating oil-bearing layers under active crossflow. A two-layer black-oil simulation model was constructed using commercial black-oil simulation software, with Layer 1 initialized at 1,000 psia and Layer 2 at 3,500 psia to create a controlled and physically representative pressure imbalance that induces inter-layer fluid communication. A systematic one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis across five key reservoir and fluid parameters—porosity (ϕ), horizontal permeability in x- and y- directions (Kx, KY), API gravity, and oil viscosity (µo)—generated 574 dimensionless simulation data points. Nonlinear regression in commercial statistical software yielded a six-parameter power-law additive correlation validated by a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.904, Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.596%, and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.772. The physical significance of each regression coefficient is interpreted with direct engineering relevance: viscosity dominates the model with an exponent of -7.623; vertical permeability carries the only positive exponent (+0.456), representing its role as the inter-layer communication conduit; and API gravity exhibits a reversed trend under crossflow conditions—lighter oil enhancing the crossflow drive and paradoxically reducing individual- layer deliverability. An explicit applicability domain is defined for all nine model parameters. A step-by-step practical application workflow is provided to enable direct field use. The correlation provides a practical screening and forecasting tool for multilayer well deliverability assessment where crossflow complicates conventional IPR analysis, and its performance is benchmarked against the Vogel IPR baseline.

title: Benchmarking Time Series Foundation Models for Oil and Gas Data Forecasting and Well Event Detection
abstract: Forecasting and event detection in oil and gas operations are critical for maintaining flow assurance and equipment health, yet traditional analytical models often struggle with complex, non-linear time-series data. This study evaluates the efficacy of a newly developed time series foundation model against existing state-of-the-art foundation models for forecasting operational sensor dynamics across diverse well event regimes. Performance is benchmarked using open-source operational datasets, specifically a flowloop laboratory dataset representing multiphase flow slugging, and a comprehensive offshore dataset covering regular flow, unstable flow, severe slugging, and rapid productivity loss scenarios. Results indicate that the proposed model generally outperforms the baseline models, demonstrating superior accuracy in forecasting typical periodic or semi-periodic patterns associated with severe slugging flow, as well as tracking the slow progression of degrading equipment conditions. However, the evaluation also highlights specific limitations; the proposed model is less effective under conditions where operational changes are sudden and abrupt, scenarios in which alternative models exhibit lower error rates. Ultimately, this benchmarking highlights the strengths of specialized foundation models for predictive maintenance and flow assurance, while outlining areas for future algorithmic refinement in handling abrupt transient events.
