title: Recovery of soil nitrogen by maize at various soil depths: a field study using 15N-labelled fertiliser nitrogen
abstract: Nitrogen (N) recovery by maize (Zea mays L.) in harvested grain is typically only 30–45% of applied fertiliser N, with the remainder susceptible to leaching and denitrification. In New Zealand, nitrate-loss regulation has increased reliance on nutrient budgeting models such as OverseerFM®, which until recently assumed a maximum effective maize rooting depth of 60 cm, potentially under-representing N uptake by deep-rooted crops, e.g., maize. Using 15N labelled fertiliser, maize uptake, timing and partitioning of absorbed N from soil depths of 60, 90, and 120 cm were assessed under New Zealand field conditions. A two year field experiment was conducted on a Waikato allophanic soil, with 15N applied at the V6 growth stage via subsurface injection beneath individual plants. Plant tissues were sampled through to maturityto trace depth specific uptake and redistribution. Recovery of 15N in aboveground biomass mostly occurred post-silking, and was 65-69%. Results show that maize can access soil N from ≥120 cm depth, supporting improved representation of deep rooting and late-season N uptake in nutrient budgeting models.

title: Improving crop nitrogen uptake prediction in OverseerFM through iterative soil-crop coupling and recalibration
abstract: OverseerFM is widely used for farm nutrient budgeting in New Zealand. Earlier versions under-predicted cropnitrogen (N) uptake for some crops under moderate to high soil N supply, leaving more residual N in the simulated soil profile and limiting the model’s ability to represent the environmental benefits of catch crops and other cropping systems. To address this, field data from 37 experiments across a range of crop types and regions were used to recalibrate crop parameters. Two updates were introduced: a luxury N uptake factor to represent additional uptake when N supply exceeded baseline requirements, and an iterative monthly coupling between crop uptake and soil mineral N supply. Together, these changes reduced under-prediction of above-ground N uptake and improved agreement withobservations across diverse crops, including reduced prediction error in an independent validation dataset. Soil-mineral-N prediction error also decreased in one rotation dataset, although substantial discrepancies remained. The revised model therefore provides a stronger basis for representing N capture by catch crops, while winter-period uptake and nitrate leaching require further validation.

title: Decadal trends in plantation Pinus radiata (D. Don) forest growth
abstract: Plantation Pinus radiata (D. Don) forests are longterm crops uniquely exposed to climate change; trees planted today and harvested after 2050 will experience multiple cycles of variable rainfall, along with an anticipated increase of another approximately 100 ppm in atmospheric CO2 (eCO2) and associated warming. While process-based modelling has suggested substantial increases in tree growth in higher-rainfall regions, empirical model outputs indicate the rate ofincreases in productivity has slowed. We analysed three decades (1992–2022) of growth data across permanentP. radiata plots in New Zealand to quantify recent trends in plantation productivity and to assess the implications of any decline for the sector, farm forestry and the wider economy. P. radiata growth increased by 25% from the 1990s to the 2000s but plateaued to a <5% gain in the 2010s, despite predicted benefits from rising eCO2, and continued adoption of improved germplasm, silvicultural practices and the practice of planting on landscapes with a pastoral history. Theage-class distribution became increasingly skewed towards recently established and younger plantations in later decades, which may partially mask underlyingchanges in productivity. These findings indicate that gains in forest productivity have slowed, highlighting the need for more targeted management interventions to maximise the benefits of eCO2 through efficient water and nutrient supply and utilisation.

title: National and regional economic impacts of climate-driven pasture decline
abstract: Declining pasture and crop harvests is increasingly evident across several New Zealand regions. Milk production per cow has continued to increase over the past two decades, driven largely through increased use of supplementary feed. This may mask the true effect of declining pasture and crop harvested, which remains fundamental to profitable dairy production. Pasture is the cheapest form of feed for a dairy farm, and relying on other feeds will erode New Zealand’scompetitive cost advantage. This study quantifies the national and regional economic costs of declining pasture and crop harvested and estimates the potential value of strategic investment in forage and farmsystem solutions. Using the Dairy Sector Pathways model, parameterised with DairyBase and Dairy Statistics data, four scenarios were simulated to 2064/65: a baseline holding pasture and crop harvested constant; a business‑as‑usual scenario with declining pasture andcrop harvested; a strategic mitigation scenario slowing the decline; and an improvement scenario increasing pasture and crop harvested. Outcomes were assessed using discounted net present values of operating profit for dairy farms. Nationally, pasture decline imposes an estimated net present value cost of $10.5 billion to the 2064/65 season, relative to a Baseline net present value of $98.6 billion. Strategic investment generates positive economic returns relative to business-as-usual, valued at $0.5 billion under mitigation and $2.6 billion under improvement. Benefits depended strongly on the timing and extent of technology uptake, highlighting the importance of early and widespread investment tosustain pasturebased dairy systems.

title: GIS-Based Optimal Site Selection of Agricultural By-Product Resource Recovery Facilities for Smart Agricultural and Livestock Systems: A Case Study of Naju-si and Goheung-gun, Jeollanam-do, South Korea
abstract: The importance of producing bioenergy using agricultural by-products is increasing in response to energy depletion and climate change caused by dependence on fossil fuels. In particular, rice straw is one of the most abundant agricultural by-products generated in Korea and has high potential for utilization in various bioenergy resource recovery applications. The objective of this study was to estimate rice straw production and select optimal locations for agricultural by-product resource recovery facilities based on resource availability, facility processing capacity, and collection and transportation costs. Field measurements of soil properties were conducted to analyze their relationships with rice straw production, while rice cultivation and production statistics were obtained from the Korean Statistical Information Service (KOSIS), and digital map data were obtained from the National Geographic Information Institute (NGII). The soil-property data were statistically analyzed to evaluate their relationships with rice straw production, while the digital map data were processed using ArcGIS Pro to delineate paddy field areas, apply correction factors based on statistical rice cultivation areas, generate representative centroid locations, identify candidate sites using spatial exclusion criteria, and calculate road-network-based transportation distances and costs. However, since the economic feasibility of resource recovery facilities is greatly affected by the stable supply of raw materials and the efficiency of collection costs, optimal site selection considering resource generation and transportation characteristics is necessary. The suitability of rice cultivation was evaluated by investigating the soil moisture content, electrical conductivity (EC), penetration resistance, and soil texture of the study area, and the resource supply was estimated based on the rice cultivation area and rice straw generation in 2024. In addition, ArcGIS Pro 3.6.4 (Esri, Redlands, CA, USA) was used to derive candidate sites by considering conditions such as roads, slope, streams, rivers, lakes, and wetlands, and the optimal locations by facility scale were evaluated by analyzing the total logistics costs, including collection and transportation costs. The results showed that both study areas exhibited soil properties suitable for rice cultivation and were capable of providing a stable supply of rice straw. For the 30,000 ton processing facility, two optimal locations were selected in each of Naju-si and Goheung-gun, while one optimal location was selected in each region for the 60,000 ton processing facility. The GIS-based site selection method proposed in this study is expected to be applicable not only to rice straw resource recovery facilities but also to the planning and supply chain development of various agricultural biomass resource recovery facilities. It is also expected to contribute to the development of efficient systems for achieving sustainable agriculture and carbon neutrality.

title: Thermal Sensing for Crop Water-Status Assessment and Precision Irrigation: Methods, Scale Effects, and Decision Pathways
abstract: Efficient irrigation management requires reliable identification of when and where crop water limitations occur, followed by the conversion of diagnostic information into practical management actions. Thermal sensing provides a non-contact means of observing changes in canopy energy exchange associated with stomatal regulation and reduced transpiration. This review evaluates the use of thermal information across the complete decision pathway from crop water-status assessment to precision irrigation. It first examines the physiological and energy-balance mechanisms underlying canopy temperature responses and discusses how crop type, phenological stage, canopy structure, meteorological conditions, and concurrent stresses influence thermal signals. It then compares ground-based sensors, mobile systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and satellite observations in terms of temporal continuity, spatial coverage, resolution, and operational constraints. Particular attention is given to radiometric calibration, canopy extraction, mixed pixels, observation timing, reference-temperature construction, and field validation. The performance and limitations of canopy-air temperature differences, the crop water stress index, energy-balance approaches, and data-driven models are subsequently assessed. Methodologically, this review synthesizes literature systematically retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, selecting studies that explicitly integrate thermal sensing, crop water status diagnostics, and precision irrigation applications. Evidence across the reviewed studies shows that thermal measurements can support spatially explicit water-stress diagnosis, but fixed thresholds and models developed under individual experimental conditions often exhibit limited transferability across crops, seasons, and environments. More reliable irrigation decisions therefore require the integration of thermal observations with soil moisture, weather data, crop models, and phenological information. Future research should prioritize traceable calibration procedures, dynamic irrigation thresholds, uncertain-ty-aware multimodal models, and multi-season field validation. The agronomic value of thermal sensing should ultimately be evaluated through its effects on irrigation water use, crop yield, water productivity, operational cost, and system robustness.

title: Context-Dependent Effects of Lung Segmentation Preprocessing on Radiology-Report-Derived Pneumonia Classification in Chest Radiographs: A Comparative Study Across Acquisition Settings and Backbone Architectures
abstract: Lung segmentation is often used to restrict chest radiograph classifiers to pulmonary anatomy, but its observed effects may vary across acquisition settings, mask sources, and model configurations. We evaluated radiology-report-derived pneumonia classification on MIMIC-CXR-JPG across two frontal views, five input conditions (raw, MedSAM3 mask/crop, and CheXMask mask/crop), and seven backbones using patient-grouped 5-fold cross-validation with a 15% outer holdout. In anteroposterior (AP) radiographs, RAD-DINO with MedSAM3 cropping achieved the numerically highest AUROC of 0.8153 (95% CI, 0.7984–0.8316). In posteroanterior (PA) radiographs, raw EVA-X-Base achieved the numerically highest AUROC of 0.8261 (95% CI, 0.8048–0.8462). Across backbones, crop-versus-raw AUROC differences were small and heterogeneous, with none remaining statistically significant after multiplicity adjustment; equivalence or noninferiority was not formally assessed. Hard masking showed larger mean AUROC reductions in PA radiographs (−0.0141 for MedSAM3 and −0.0142 for CheXMask), with four backbone-specific PA masking contrasts remaining significant after Holm adjustment. These findings do not support a universal benefit of lung-focused preprocessing within the internally validated MIMIC-CXR-JPG cohort. Cross-backbone differences were interpreted descriptively under the shared training protocol, and the generalizability of these preprocessing effects to independent institutions and imaging populations remains to be established.

title: Rule Relaxation with Large Language Models in Agricultural Regulatory Technologies for Compliance and Permit Assessments
abstract: Rules form the foundation of regulatory systems by defining the obligations, permissions, and prohibitions that govern human activities. Regulatory processes universally rely on taking specific inputs from the stakeholders before checking them against specific rules. As regulators in various sectors such as agriculture increasingly adopt digital regulatory technologies, regulatory rules must be interpreted consistently by both humans and machines. Among the diverse rule types in legislation, quantitative rules are particularly important because they define measurable constraints that, if modified, may alter the scope of regulatory compliance. This paper presents a large language model (LLM)-based framework for analyzing rule relaxation in quantitative agricultural regulations. The proposed approach classifies quantitative rules into three categories: single-value rules, ranged or interval rules, and ratio rules. A mathematical framework is introduced to formally represent quantitative rule relaxation, while controlled numerical perturbations are applied to determine whether modifications to regulatory parameters expand, reduce, or ambiguously affect the set of actions permitted by a regulation. This methodology addresses the semantic effects of quantitative changes on deontic regulatory rules while preserving their underlying obligations and permissions. The framework is evaluated using pesticide regulations published by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA). Performance is assessed using both class- and rule-specific accuracy and macro F1 scores for multiple LLM models. The results demonstrate that LLMs can be used to interpret the semantic consequences of quantitative modifications. However, the accuracy of performance declines with the number of variables and the complexity of the rules. The proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for explainable agricultural Regulatory Technology (RegTech) systems and future Rules as Code implementations.

title: Improvements to Deep Learning-Based Object Detection Algorithms in Greenhouses
abstract: Capsicums (chili peppers), serving as critical economic crops, hold a significant role within greenhouse cultivation, driving the development of the agricultural economy. Traditional methods for detecting chili pepper flowers are notably time-consuming and labor-intensive. The unique visual characteristics of chili pepper flowers are suitable for accurate classification and identification using deep learning technology. Nevertheless, numerous challenges exist in identifying chili pepper flowers in complex backgrounds. This study proposes an edge-enhanced Normalization-based Attention Module (E-NAM), which integrates gradient and magnitude into NAM. E-NAM is embedded into the C2f (Coarse-to-Fine) module of YOLOv8 to enhance edge-awareness and feature discrimination. To enhance the model’s semantic understanding, we propose ES-SPPF (SPPF with enhanced semantic transmission), making it more suitable for small object detection. At the same time, a threshold-based piecewise IoU (PIIoU) is proposed to improve the model’s inference efficiency. Finally, dilated convolution is introduced between the backbone and the head, which helps to capture small objects by integrating local and global information. Compared with the vanilla YOLOv8, our proposed enhancements (NAM, ES-SPPF, PIIoU, and Dilated Convolution) achieve a consistent and significant improvement of 4.4% in mAP (Mean Average Precision) (from 78.2% to 82.6%) on the greenhouse chili flower dataset, while maintaining a real-time inference speed of 73 FPS (Frames Per Second). The findings can serve as an important reference for crop object detection.

title: Enhanced Machine Learning Techniques for System Imbalance Forecasting
abstract: The unpredictable nature of renewable energy sources (RES) has become a major cause of imbalance between electricity generation and demand, which the Transmission System Operator (TSO) must handle in real-time operation. The RES stochasticity and the often-excessive imbalance quantities have increased the financial risks for RES aggregators. Consequently, forecasting system imbalance has become crucial for RES aggregators who seek to avoid these charges. This paper implements contemporary real-time machine learning models to forecast system imbalance and evaluates them based on forecasting accuracy. Qualitative predictions stem from a classification problem determining the system’s direction: whether there is energy overgeneration (“long” system) or production deficit (“short” system). This prediction, combined with a regression problem’s solution and confidence interval calculations, offers deeper insight into the system imbalance quantity. A case study for the Greek power system is presented along with the respective test results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed methods for predicting both system imbalance direction and magnitude. The forecasts are further compared against naïve benchmarks and through statistical significance tests, while the probabilistic forecasts are embedded in a risk-constrained (CVaR-based) market positioning problem, which, in an ex post application for a Greek RES aggregator, yields savings of €0.98–1.34 million over a four-month period.

title: Phenotypic and Genomic Characterization of Bacillus sp. DLB3, a Black Pepper Rhizosphere Isolate with Antagonistic, Abiotic Stress-Tolerant, and Antibiotic-Susceptible Traits
abstract: Rhizosphere bacteria combining biocontrol activity with resilience to environmental stress are valuable candidates for sustainable agriculture. This study characterized strain DLB3, isolated from black pepper rhizosphere soil, through dual-culture and disk-diffusion antagonism assays, enzymatic and siderophore screening, physiological tolerance tests, antibiotic susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing, and genome mining. Phylogenomic analysis and average nucleotide identity (>97%) and digital DNA–DNA hybridization (>79%) values identified the isolate as Bacillus velezensis. The strain inhibited Fusarium falciforme, Fusarium oxysporum, and Colletotrichum gloeosporioides (47.6–71.2% radial growth inhibition) and produced an inhibition zone (8.4 mm) against Ralstonia solanacearum, alongside extracellular protease, amylase, CMCase, and catecholate-type siderophore production. DLB3 tolerated a broad range of temperatures (20–50 °C, with optimal growth at 25–40 °C, peaking at 35 °C), pH (5–9), and salinity (up to 10% NaCl), and exhibited minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 1800, 500, 450, and 250 mg L−1 for Pb, Zn, Cu, and Cr, respectively, while remaining susceptible to all nine antibiotics tested. The 3,913,361 bp draft genome was assembled into 44 contigs (N50 = 990,239 bp; L50 = 2), with 99.81% completeness and 0.12% contamination according to CheckM. It harbored 18 biosynthetic gene clusters, carbohydrate-active enzymes, peptidases, and genes associated with heavy metal resistance, broadly consistent with the observed phenotypes, as well as a homolog of the cfr methyltransferase gene (97.4% identity) that was not phenotypically expressed. These findings provide a comprehensive genomic and phenotypic profile of strain DLB3 and its biocontrol-related potential.

title: Synchronizing Water and Nutrient Supply for Crop Production: Physiological Mechanisms, Technological Pathways, and the Case for Context-Specific Management
abstract: Synchronizing water and nutrient supply is central to high-yield, resource-efficient agriculture. We define synchronization operationally along three independently assessable dimensions: temporal overlap between supply and the crop demand window, spatial co-location of delivered water and nutrients with the zone of active roots, and matching of the nutrient-release rate to the crop uptake rate. Conventional simultaneous irrigation and fertilization does not necessarily ensure spatial and temporal matching between resource supply and crop demand. This review uses a four-part framework—costs of supply–demand mismatch, root sensing and response, regulatory technologies, and context-dependent variation—to trace the shift from simultaneous application to synchronized supply. Physiologically, drought restricts nutrient uptake via diffusion, mass flow, and active transport, while nutrient deficiency suppresses water-use efficiency through reduced photosynthesis and context-dependent changes in aquaporin regulation, root hydraulics, and hormonal signaling; combined stresses cause context-dependent oxidative and hormonal interactions. Roots integrate architectural plasticity, hydrotropic and nutrient-dependent foraging, hydraulic and chemical signaling, and rhizosphere processes to coordinate resource acquisition. Water–fertilizer technologies are grouped into four complementary technological pathways: fertigation, partial root-zone drying/alternate wetting and drying, sensor- and model-driven real-time control, and controlled-release fertilizer. Their effects diverge with soil physicochemical and hydraulic properties, genotype, seasonal climate, and spatial scale, so no universally optimal scheme is supported by current evidence. Key bottlenecks are weak in situ root–soil observation, lack of coupled multi-process models, and scarce field validation. Future progress requires high-throughput root phenotyping, AI prediction, low-cost sensing, and multi-objective optimization for context-specific management.

title: Nonlinear Mathematical Modeling of Crop Growth and Biomass Accumulation for Accurate Yield Prediction in Smallholder Farming Systems
abstract: Accurate yield prediction in smallholder farming systems remains a central challenge in agricultural science, particularly across sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, where resource constraints, climate variability, and data scarcity severely limit the applicability of conventional linear models. This paper presents a comprehensive review and synthesis of nonlinear mathematical frameworks for modeling crop growth and biomass accumulation, with emphasis on their suitability for smallholder contexts. We examine logistics, Gompertz, Richards, and betafunction growth models, as well as process-based dynamic simulation approaches including APSIM, DSSAT, and AquaCrop, and evaluate their integration with remote sensing data and machine learning algorithms. Key findings indicate that hybrid models combining physiological process descriptions with data-driven optimization consistently outperform purely empirical or mechanistic approaches, particularly when calibrated with local agronomic data under variable input conditions. We further discuss parameter identifiability, model parsimony, and uncertainty quantification as critical requirements for deployment in data-limited smallholder environments. This review synthesizes evidence from 2019 to 2025 and provides a roadmap for developing robust, scalable nonlinear crop yield prediction frameworks tailored to the heterogeneous conditions of smallholder agriculture.

title: Navigating Transformative Agricultural Technologies on the Path to Food System Transformation
abstract: Modern agriculture encompasses various existing or emerging technologies, such as robotics, nanotechnology, synthetic proteins, cellular agriculture, gene-editing technologies, artificial intelligence, blockchain, and machine learning, which can have a significant transformative impact on the future of agricultural and food systems. These technologies underpin concepts such as vertical farming, digital agriculture, the bioeconomy, circular agriculture, and aquaponics. Examples of these concepts include different strands of agroecology, such as permaculture, regenerative agriculture, and ecological intensification, which may themselves require the use of various technologies and often incorporate indigenous knowledge. These approaches can also be connected to and integrated with digital technologies. This requires responsible innovation processes that entail anticipating the potential impacts of agricultural technologies through inclusive processes, as well as responding to emerging outcomes and adjusting the direction and course of transition pathways. This paper emphasizes the need to pay greater attention to the inclusion and exclusion effects associated with agricultural technologies and to anticipate their potential impacts through inclusive processes.

title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

title: Resource-Optimal Screening for Two-Tier Quantum System Characterization
abstract: Quantum processing units (QPUs) require frequent benchmarking to track hardware drift, yet standard protocols such as randomized benchmarking are resource-intensive and compete with application workloads for scarce QPU time. We present a resource-optimal screening strategy that combines a two-tier, risk-based testing architecture with optimal experiment design: a lightweight screening probe runs regularly and triggers expensive full characterization only when statistically significant change is detected, while the probe itself is designed to maximize detection sensitivity under explicit resource constraints. For an exponential fidelity model, we derive closed-form optimal circuit sizes and introduce an effective gate count that renders the analysis hardware-independent. We instantiate the strategy for two applications. For gate-quality verification, we show that optimally designed screening probes outperform randomized benchmarking with optimal experimental design (OED) by more than 4$\times$ in detection rate at equal resource cost. For compiler benchmarking, we formalize compiler comparison as a paired hypothesis test and derive the optimal circuit size for distinguishing compilation strategies. Despite their different observables and test statistics, both applications yield structurally the same closed-form expression for the optimal probe circuit size as a function of gate fidelity, illustrating the generality of the framework. Numerical and hardware experiments on QPUs (Rigetti Ankaa-3, IQM Garnet, IQM Emerald) confirm the theoretical predictions, with observed optimal circuit sizes matching the derived values across all devices.

title: A superprocess model for eDNA transport in random river environment
abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) is increasingly used to monitor aquatic organisms in rivers, yet predicting its concentration and assessing the reliability of such predictions remain challenging because river flow fluctuates with long memory and models of eDNA dynamics are inevitably misspecified. We propose a stochastic modeling framework for eDNA concentration in rivers that addresses both issues. The eDNA concentration is described by a stochastic partial differential equation with transport, decay, source, and square-root multiplicative noise, and the flow velocity is modeled by a superposition of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type processes with long memory. We show that the long memory of the flow velocity induces superdiffusive transport of eDNA, with the variance of the transported distance growing superlinearly in the ensemble sense. The proposed model admits a closed-form Laplace functional, based on which we prove the existence and uniqueness in law of the solution on an unbounded domain. We further evaluate the effects of model uncertainty through a robust control formulation based on the relative entropy, in which the lower and upper bounds of the expected eDNA concentration, together with the worst-case distortions, are obtained in closed form. The framework is applied to eDNA and flow velocity data collected for the upstream migration of Plecoglossus altivelis altivelis in a river in Japan. The results demonstrate that the closed-form bounds provide a computationally inexpensive tool for quantifying the range of eDNA concentrations that can be expected under model uncertainty.

title: Extended LASMP: Language Aided Subset Sampling Based Motion Planner for Drone Navigation
abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.

title: Stochastic quantization and Osterwalder-Schrader axioms for quantum field theory models
abstract: This PhD thesis constructs the $P(Φ)_2$ Euclidean quantum field theory on $\mathscr{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$. We first construct the finite-volume measure of the $P(Φ)_2$ model on $\mathscr{D}'(\mathbb{S}_R)$, where $\mathbb{S}_R$ is a two-dimensional sphere of radius $R\in\mathbb{N}_+$. To this end, we rely on Nelson's hypercontractivity estimate. We then use parabolic stochastic quantization and the energy method to construct the infinite-volume measure on $\mathscr{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$. This requires establishing the global-in-time existence of solutions to the corresponding stochastic partial differential equations with fixed cutoffs. The remainder of the thesis is devoted to verifying the Osterwalder-Schrader axioms: regularity, reflection positivity, and invariance under translations, rotations, and reflections. This combination of axioms, which is crucial for obtaining a non-trivial local relativistic quantum field theory on Minkowski spacetime, had not been established in earlier constructions based on stochastic quantization.

title: Distributional Counterfactual Dependence in the Special Sciences
abstract: Special-science explanations often concern distributions rather than individual outcomes. Since higher-level states depend on lower-level processes, what would make a higher-level explanation redundant? I argue that redundancy requires replacement without loss, not merely a reconstruction of individual outcomes. Distributional counterfactual dependence (DCD) identifies how changes in higher-level conditions alter an outcome distribution or a relevant feature of it. Against the background of stochastic supervenience, I distinguish this explanatory role from the dependence of higher-level states on lower-level bases. A replacement must be specified independently of the distribution to be explained and preserve the same counterfactual pattern at the grain and across the conditions relevant to the question. Applications to wage distributions, cognitive load, and selection clarify this requirement. A hypothetical comparison shows how a lower-level model can preserve the explanation and why matching selected outcome statistics may not suffice. DCD thus describes one form of non-reductive explanation that depends on counterfactual organization rather than additional higher-level productive powers.

title: Self-Supervised Passive WiFi CSI-Based Motion Tracking with Physics-Informed Deep SSM
abstract: Inferring target position from WiFi channel state information (CSI) is challenging due to the noisy and heterogeneous nature of CSI-derived observations. Measurements such as angle, delay, and Doppler provide only imperfect information about target position and velocity, particularly in dynamic multipath environments where observation reliability varies. Motivated by this challenge, this paper proposes a physics-informed Bayesian state space framework for passive CSI-based tracking. We introduce a context-conditioned deep state space model (DSSM) that captures temporal motion and environmental dynamics, while adaptively modeling time-varying observation uncertainties. By incorporating geometric constraints, this framework enables heterogeneous CSI measurement modalities to jointly regularize the consistency and confidence of the tracking process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields smoother trajectory estimates with reduced temporal fluctuations and outperforms existing methods in tracking accuracy.

title: Can LLMs Trust Appropriately? Evaluating Calibrated Reliance on Imperfect Partners
abstract: Large language models increasingly collaborate with humans and peer AI agents whose contributions may be incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect. Effective collaboration requires calibrated trust, whereby decisions to rely on, verify, or assist a partner adapt rationally as empirical evidence accumulates. We investigate whether models translate partner evidence into appropriate reliance policies. We introduce a benchmark of 324 scenarios across 23 collaboration categories. Each scenario involves three sequential decisions with explicit transition dynamics, feedback emissions, and cost schedules, permitting exact analytical evaluation of choices against their expected consequences over the remaining interaction. Evaluating seven models alongside 36 controlled-history probes, we dissociate evidence sensitivity from normatively appropriate action. While the strongest frontier model approaches near-optimal decisions, other models exhibit recurring pathologies: procuring excessive safeguards, purchasing verification tests with zero expected value of information, prioritizing immediate savings over cooperative learning, and misallocating assistance to suboptimal channels. Supplying explicit posterior distributions resolves certain errors while introducing new failure modes. Calibrated trust in autonomous agents critically demands coupling empirical evidence with forward-looking decision utility.

title: HumanoidNDM: Closing the Training-Deployment Gap of Motion Tracking via Humanoid Neural Dynamics Model
abstract: Humanoid robots have recently achieved remarkable success in motion tracking. However, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter dynamics gaps arising from either extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling, resulting in a significant training-deployment gap. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune policies represents the crucial last mile for robust deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose HumanoidNDM, an online fine-tuning framework for humanoid motion tracking driven by a real-world-trained neural dynamics model. First, in the data collection stage, we introduce a low-frequency reference perturbation method with an adaptive intensity mechanism, balancing deployment feasibility and exploration efficiency. Second, for the model training stage, we train a robust history-based, proprioceptive neural dynamics model in Euclidean space by incorporating differentiable forward kinematics, eliminating the reliance on costly motion capture systems. Finally, in the policy fine-tuning stage, we directly fine-tune the policy via backpropagated model gradients, achieving high data efficiency. Through physical validation on the Unitree G1 robot, we demonstrate that HumanoidNDM enables rapid real-world adaptation to various perturbations, representing the first online, MoCap-free fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies.

title: AGENS: Agentic Link Construction for Environment and Intent Aware 6G Communication
abstract: The emergence of diverse intelligent services is driving 6G networks toward an intelligent communication ecosystem with increasingly complex operating scenarios. However, existing AI-based communication methods mainly focus on isolated tasks or individual physical-layer mod- ules, which is insufficient for AI-native 6G systems that must jointly perceive dynamic environments, understand specific user intents, coordinate multiple coupled PHY-layer modules, and remain compatible with existing communication infrastructures. To address this gap, this paper, for the first time, explores auto- matic environment- and intent-aware full-link construction, which aims to generate executable PHY-layer configurations according to channel conditions and service requirements. We propose AGENS, an agentic communication decision-making framework for AI-native 6G link construction. Rather than replacing the existing PHY-layer protocol stack with a black-box end-to-end model, AGENS operates on top of the modular communication framework and jointly optimizes end-to-end PHY-layer configu- rations. Specifically, AGENS encodes CSI and natural-language user instructions, aligns communication states with user intents through cross-modal fusion, and leverages a pretrained LLM for intent-aware reasoning. An LSTM-based sequential action generator further captures dependencies among coupled sub- actions and produces structured full-link strategies. To enable stable training in the high-dimensional discrete action space, AGENS adopts a two-stage learning framework, where heuristic supervised initialization is followed by multi-objective reinforce- ment learning to jointly optimize reliability, throughput, and power consumption.

title: Convergence Analysis of Variable-Separation-Based Model Reduction for Linear Parametric Partial Differential Equations
abstract: This paper analyzes the convergence of a variable-separation (VS) model reduction method that successively constructs separated approximations to the solutions of linear parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) by solving residual problems at sampled parameter values. We prove that the resulting VS approximations converge almost surely to the exact parametric solution in the parameter-averaged energy norm, under finite-dimensional approximation conditions on the error family and the assumptions of symmetry, uniform coercivity, and uniform boundedness of the governing bilinear forms. For parametric PDEs whose operators and right-hand sides admit finite-term separated representations, we construct finite-dimensional approximation spaces for the error family and bound their dimensions and approximation errors, thereby verifying these approximation conditions and obtaining an $O((\log N)^{-1})$ upper bound for the expected parameter-averaged error energy after $N$ iterations. When the solution families are contained in a fixed finite-dimensional space, we obtain the sharper $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the expected error energy and, if the operator is also parameter-independent, exact recovery for almost every parameter after an almost surely finite number of iterations. Numerical experiments illustrate the error decay of the VS approximations, as well as finite-step recovery in the parameter-independent case.

title: Edge-Centric Adaptive Neural Activation via Parametric Tanh Functions
abstract: Within the broader landscape of artificial intelligence architectures, this paper introduces a compact, edge-centric neural framework that resolves the computational bottlenecks of modern edge-activated paradigms like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) while retaining their expressiveness over traditional Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). While KANs demonstrate remarkable representational capacity by placing learnable univariate functions on connection edges rather than hidden nodes, their reliance on non-local B-splines introduces severe optimization hurdles, high memory overhead, and poor hardware scaling. To bridge this gap, we propose the Parametric Tanh Connection Function, a smooth, bounded architectural primitive defined as $a_{\tanh}(x;δ,α,β,γ) = δ+ α\tanh(βx + γ)$. This formulation unifies offset, amplitude, local slope, and horizontal displacement into a lightweight, 4-parameter differentiable mapping optimized edge-by-edge via backpropagation. Evaluated on dense architectures using MNIST and CIFAR-10, our parametric tanh connection model achieves significant absolute accuracy gains over traditional affine baselines-reaching 95.63% $\pm$ 0.08% on MNIST and 44.74% $\pm$ 0.18% on CIFAR-10. Crucially, it matches or exceeds the expressiveness of unconstrained 7-parameter exponential connection baselines while requiring up to 85% less training runtime. By replacing complex splines or hyper-flexible exponents with a bounded, analytically smooth hyperbolic tangent kernel, this work delivers a highly scalable, hardware-friendly compromise for heterogeneous connection-level deep learning.

title: Modelling Emotional Dynamics in the Life of Amrita Pritam: A Nonlinear Perspective on Longing and Companionship
abstract: Amrita Pritam (1919-2005) was a prominent writer of modern Indian literature, particularly in Punjabi and Hindi. Her literary-biographical context provides a setting for exploring memory, longing, companionship, and emotional regulation through simple dynamical models. This study develops three single-state ordinary differential equation models centred on two important relational references in her life: Sahir Ludhianvi, associated with memory, absence, recollection, and longing, and Imroz, associated with companionship, care, continuity, and support. The first model describes Sahir-related longing through memory-driven excitation and natural emotional decay (fading); the second models Imroz-related companionship through nonlinear stabilisation around a preferred emotional state; and the third unifies both influences within a single-state framework. Analytical solutions, equilibrium conditions, local stability analysis, and numerical simulations are used to examine emotional-state decay and persistence, convergence to stable equilibria, and threshold effects on system behaviour. The results indicate that memory-related reinforcement may sustain the modelled emotional state under suitable stimulus conditions, whereas Imroz-related companionship may drive the system towards a stable upper equilibrium when initial conditions lie within the admissible range. The unified model illustrates how memory-driven longing and companionship-driven stabilisation associated with Sahir and Imroz can jointly shape a modelled emotional trajectory. This study is conceptual and mathematical, not empirical or psychological. It neither measures private emotions of Amrita Pritam nor estimates parameters from biographical data. Instead, it introduces a simple nonlinear framework for exploring memory, fading, companionship, equilibrium, and threshold effects in a literary-biographical context.

title: Timing Matters Twice: When to Query and When to Skip in Flow-Matching On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) enables flow-matching models to acquire complementary capabilities from specialized teachers through supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, different evaluation dimensions, such as aesthetics and OCR accuracy, and different tasks, such as image generation and editing, emphasize different aspects of the denoising process, suggesting that their effective supervision may occur at different stages. Existing methods typically select supervision states from predefined timestep distributions, which may overlook these phase-dependent differences and incur unnecessary computational overhead. This motivates two critical timing decisions: when to adaptively query teachers for effective supervision based on the evolving generative process, and when to skip the remaining rollout to avoid redundant computation. In this paper, we introduce PhaseOPD, a phase-aware query-and-skip framework that identifies generative phases online from revisions of predicted-clean latents, using existing student velocity predictions without additional model evaluations. For each task-assigned teacher, PhaseOPD selects a supervision state based on its phase preference and skips the unused rollout suffix once all query decisions are finalized, preserving the single-query velocity-distillation objective. On SD3.5-M, PhaseOPD executes only 5.56 of 16 rollout positions per local batch, reducing training time by 41.3% relative to DanceOPD while improving Aesthetic, GenEval, and OCR scores.

title: Numerical Construction of Quasi-Periodic Solutions for Nonlinear PDEs: II. Unbounded Perturbation
abstract: Many nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in physical models involve unbounded perturbations, where nonlinear terms contain spatial derivatives. Such perturbations can be expressed as compositions of unbounded operators with bounded nonlinear maps. In this paper, we propose alternating numerical schemes for constructing quasi-periodic solutions to this class of PDEs, including the nonlinear acoustic wave (NLAW) equation and the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation. To render the nonlinear perturbations bounded, we apply inverse differential operators as a preconditioning; this, however, also rescales the linear part by polynomial factors in the spatial mode $n$. Two main difficulties arise. The first is to control the measure of the resulting ``bad'' frequencies, since the bounds on the measures of the excluded frequency sets are enlarged by polynomial factors in $n$; we show that this measure nevertheless remains small. The second concerns resonances involving the perturbed eigenvalues of the linearized operator at large scales. Our key observation is that, when the dispersive frequencies grow polynomially in $n$ with degree greater than one, such resonances cannot occur if the magnitude of the temporal index lies below a threshold proportional to $|n|$ raised to one less than that degree. It therefore suffices to consider the complementary regime, in which the growth induced by the unbounded perturbation can be controlled in terms of the temporal index. At large scales, an additional complication arises: for a given spatial index $n$, all temporal indices in a box may be ``bad''. We show, however, that at each scale there is at most one such spatial index. Consequently, the resulting counting loss is only polynomial and can be absorbed into the exponential-logarithmic threshold, allowing us once again to retain control over the measures of the excluded frequency sets.

title: ADReasoner: Acoustic-Linguistic Cue-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Explainable Alzheimer's Disease Detection from Speech
abstract: Speech-based Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection holds significant promise due to its scalable and non-invasive nature. However, current Speech Large Language Models (SpeechLLMs), similar to conventional AD detection systems, still treat AD detection primarily as a simple categorical classification task. This paradigm provides limited interpretability of predictions, while leaving the inherent expressiveness and reasoning capabilities of SpeechLLMs largely underutilized. In this work, we take the first step toward reframing AD detection as a deep reasoning task via Reinforcement Learning (RL). We propose ADReasoner, an RL-enhanced SpeechLLM designed to generate accurate diagnostic predictions with interpretable rationales grounded in fine-grained acoustic-linguistic cues. To achieve this, we first systematically construct ADCoT-7K, an AD speech reasoning dataset combining real data and our quality-filtered synthetic data, where each instance features Chain-of-Thought (CoT) annotations and detailed captions. Second, observing the weak perception of AD-related acoustic-linguistic cues in current SpeechLLMs, we leverage Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to develop a cue-perception-enhanced foundation model, ADReasoner-Base, thereby improving AD speech understanding. Third, alongside two standard rule-based rewards, we introduce a reasoning reward and a reasoning-label consistency reward into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for RL. Furthermore, a shrinkage mechanism is employed to suppress misleading reasoning signals, while a gating mechanism progressively introduces both rewards to stabilize policy training. Experiments on three AD datasets (Pitt, PROCESS-1, PROCESS-2) demonstrate that ADReasoner outperforms previous state-of-the-art models in both detection performance and explanation quality, advancing AD detection toward interpretable reasoning from speech.

title: CropReward: A Human-Preference Benchmark and Reward Model for Aesthetic Image Cropping
abstract: Aesthetic image cropping (AIC) aims to improve image composition and aesthetic quality by removing extraneous or distracting content. Over the past decade, AIC methods have evolved from specialized vision models to multimodal large language models(MLLMs). Reliable evaluation that reflects human preferences is essential for benchmarking AIC methods and guiding model optimization. However, the current AIC evaluation relies largely on geometry-based metrics such as intersection over union (IoU), as well as image aesthetic assessment(IAA) models. Although inconsistencies with human preferences have long been observed, the robustness and reliability of these evaluation criteria remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we first construct CropBench, a large-scale benchmark comprising 106,995 human preference pairs for 1,019 images, with each candidate set containing the original image and candidate crops produced by 14 AIC methods. A systematic study on CropBench reveals that the existing criteria, ranging from IoU to off-the-shelf IAA assessment models, only exhibit limited alignment with human preferences. Building upon CropBench, we further propose CropReward, an MLLM-based reward model that evaluates a candidate crop by comparing with the original uncropped image and outputs a score indicating explicit aesthetic improvement or degradation relative to the original. In addition, we employ CropReward to construct CropReward-300k, the largest AIC dataset to date, and further develop CropAlign, a preference-aligned AIC model trained solely with CropReward supervision, without human-annotated crop boxes. Experimental results demonstrate that CropReward aligns with human preferences significantly better than AIC existing criteria. CropAlign also surpasses the state-of-the-art AIC methods, demonstrating the advantage of CropReward in guiding AIC model optimization.

title: Honesty Testing of LLMs and AI Agents: A Vision for Software Engineering
abstract: Human oversight of large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) agents increasingly depends on their reports. Claims that conflict with a system's own judgments can conceal failures, prevent timely intervention, and contribute to severe harm. Greater autonomy makes faithful reporting increasingly important for maintaining human control. In this vision paper, we propose honesty testing of LLMs and AI agents as a new research area in software engineering. Building on existing honesty evaluations, our goal is to make faithful reporting a software quality requirement that developers can specify, test, and maintain. We define honesty bugs as behavioural defects in which an LLM or AI agent, when required to communicate faithfully, makes an explicit claim that conflicts with its own judgment at the time of reporting. We present an initial framework covering LLM-level testing under controlled inputs and agent-level testing of complete systems. The framework connects these levels to testing workflows and oracle evidence. We identify research directions in benchmarks, model and harness analysis, oracle construction, and lifecycle testing to support effective oversight alongside task correctness.

title: NameTrap: Steering AI Coding Agents Toward Security Vulnerabilities via Variable Names
abstract: AI coding agents routinely clone repositories, install packages, and read source code obtained from the Web, so publicly hosted code becomes part of the context that shapes the code they write. We show that this Web-borne context can be weaponized without any explicit instruction. We present NameTrap, a source-code poisoning attack that only renames identifiers in third-party Python files to steer AI coding agents toward attacker-targeted Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) vulnerabilities. An attacker-side coding agent iteratively aligns identifiers with a CWE-specific naming convention and confirms through local probe completions that the renamed file elicits the target weakness, while the released bait contains neither instructions nor vulnerable statements. We evaluate NameTrap across six AI coding agents, ten underlying language models, and four vulnerability categories: CWE-78, CWE-79, CWE-327, and CWE-502. Starting from files whose clean versions never yield the targeted CWE, identifier-level manipulation achieves overall attack success rates of 22.5\% to 56.0\% across the six agents, reaching 75.0\% for certain agent--model configurations, and substantially outperforms random renaming, neutral renaming, and the prior identifier-poisoning attack XOXO. The attack remains effective under Traditional Chinese prompts and transfers across models, while a security-reminder defense fails to consistently prevent vulnerability introduction. Moreover, three AI-based security analyzers and four static analyzers report none of the targeted weaknesses in the poisoned files. These findings expose an overlooked attack surface of agents that consume Web content: seemingly harmless variable names in untrusted, Web-hosted code can compromise the security of downstream software.

title: Birth-Death Structural Learning for 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a standard representation for real-time novel-view synthesis. Yet, its quality-efficiency trade-off still relies heavily on adaptive density control. Existing cloning, splitting, and pruning rules use proxy signals, such as position gradients, opacity, and image-space error. Although effective in practice, these signals do not directly answer the structural question behind density control: where should new Gaussians be allocated to reduce the multi-view reconstruction loss, and which existing primitives can be pruned with minimal penalty. To address this, we propose first-variation birth-death control for 3DGS, a principled approach that replaces heuristic structural decisions with a variational score derived from the reconstruction loss. At each structural update, we freeze the current Gaussian population, attach auxiliary mass coordinates to each primitive, and differentiate the multiview loss with respect to these coordinates. We demonstrate that this score is a coordinate of the first variation of the Splat Regression Model, giving a rigorous local descent surrogate for birth-death moves: high-score Gaussians are selected as birth sites, while low-score, low-opacity Gaussians are selected for removal. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, integrating this score into 3DGS-MCMC yields state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and outperforms existing methods, delivering the most significant gains under tight Gaussian budgets. Ultimately, our work provides compelling evidence that gradient-based variational metrics offer a principled alternative to proxy heuristics in 3DGS.

title: Optimal ratcheting dividend policies with resets
abstract: We study an optimal dividend policy problem under ratcheting and bankruptcy constraints. Firms face a tradeoff between the negative signal of a dividend reduction and a potential future bankruptcy. In contrast to previous works, the dividend rate is allowed to decrease after incurring a negative impact on equity valuation in accordance with a large empirical literature on the topic. We provide an explicit necessary and sufficient condition for the finiteness of the value function and prove the differentiability of the value function, and its characterization via viscosity solutions and the so-called supercontact property. The value function is given by the solution of a two-dimensional variational inequality combining optimal stopping, singular and impulse controls. We show that the problem is equivalent to a one-dimensional setup simplifying both mathematical and financial analysis. Finally, we provide a numerical study of the model and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the model parameters. We show the relevance of over-reaction to financial news on the manager's optimal policy.

title: A Computationally Efficient Non-Interpolation Virtual Trellis Approach for Mammogram Gradient-based Patterns Analysis
abstract: Feature analysis is a crucial step in medical image analysis, particularly in breast cancer classification. Traditional image analysis methods often struggle with optimal patterns along the diagonal axis, computational efficiency and feature buffer storage. Different classical operators require high-efficiency hardware for the complex operations, such as image convolution and gradient analysis, which are used for processing complex machine learning models for training and test operations. Here, in this research, we introduce a non-interpolation virtual trellis-based (NVHT) operator that utilizes a filter kernel over the same square image without transformation to a hexagonal trellis. This proposed method is very efficient in reducing computational and storage costs. The proposed operator is used for improved feature extraction efficiency and accuracy in disease classification. This method outperforms conventional approaches by leveraging a hexagonal pixel representation while maintaining high sensitivity in different directions with less storage.

title: Pricing Information in Search with Nonobligatory Inspection
abstract: As AI agents reshape Web search and advertising, platforms can monetize information that improves decisions. We study information pricing for sequential search among independent alternatives with nonobligatory inspection: the buyer may select any alternative without buying its report. We show that a common fee maximizes static revenue for identical priors, resolving a uniform-pricing conjecture. Our results also establish that exact optimization is NP-hard for heterogeneous binary priors. Despite this hardness, our polynomial-time static pricing algorithm achieves a $3$-approximation to the information surplus. More generally, a common static fee approximates optimal adaptive revenue within a logarithmic factor in the number of alternatives. This guarantee is asymptotically tight.

title: ParetoRSI-Gym: Can AI Agents Improve Language Models Across Multiple Domains?
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.

title: Path-Specific Geometric-Stochastic Channel Model for Scattering from ISAC Targets: A Unified Measurement-Based Characterization of Robots, Humans, and Automobiles at 28 GHz
abstract: This paper develops a channel model for scattering from a broad class of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) targets-robots, humans, and automobiles-based on a unified measurement campaign at 28~GHz. Nine targets are characterized from numerous transmitter--receiver configurations per target, spanning full bistatic and aspect angles and thus covering backward to forward scattering. Repeated acquisitions are collected for each configuration to capture target motion and dynamics, yielding nearly 117\,000 acquisitions in total. Measurements are collected with a 2~GHz-wide channel sounder equipped with a 256-element phased-array antenna, followed by digital beamforming and super-resolution processing for reliable extraction of multiple paths in delay and 2D angle, with average estimation errors of 0.1~ns and 0.2$^\circ$ respectively. From these measurements, we reduce a \emph{path-specific} channel representation in which the scattering is modeled as a cluster of paths whose center is defined by the bistatic specular \emph{geometry}; the cluster shape is described \emph{stochastically}. To ensure physically grounded spatio--temporal consistency, extracted paths are mapped to incident points on the target, each with an associated radar cross section (RCS) that is compatible with the 3GPP TR~38.901 ISAC channel model, and are subsequently mapped back to path properties for channel synthesis. The resulting statistical distributions are well behaved, physically interpretable, and consistent across targets, geometries, and motion. Comparison between measured and synthesized channel realizations demonstrates close agreement in pathloss trends and fluctuation behavior. Together, these results yield a high-fidelity, measurement-derived channel representation suitable for ISAC simulation, target modeling, and system design.

title: CyberDual: AI Attackers versus AI Code Reviewers in Real Software Maintenance
abstract: Open-source projects now let AI agents review incoming code, but the code under review may itself come from an AI attacker. We present CyberDual, an arena for this dual role of AI: attacker agents hide an exploitable bug in real maintenance work on widely used open-source projects, and reviewer agents try to find and repair it. Execution decides each match: we rerun the attacker's proof of concept (PoC) on the code that comes out of review. Every attack is new, and the windows can be rebuilt each quarter from the latest upstream history. Three agentic reviewers catch 85-91% of 1,088 valid attacks from six attackers. Yet when the attacker spreads the bug over real upstream commits, about one in six attack slots still ends with a working exploit after review. The strongest attacker has open weights: GLM 5.3 almost never refuses, and its attacks make up 13 of the 28 that get past all three reviewers. When they miss, Claude reviewers mostly approve the attack, while GPT-6-Sol mostly repairs the wrong code; a reviewer from a second vendor catches about two thirds of a Claude reviewer's misses. Beyond a leaderboard, CyberDual has three uses. First, PoC execution gives both sides a reward that agent reports cannot game, so its surviving attacks can train reviewers against stronger attackers. Second, it can gate a release on both scores: Claude Sonnet 5 refuses one in five attack slots, yet attacks about as well as GPT-6-Sol, so refusal alone does not remove attack capability. Third, it can warn the teams behind a deployed reviewer when a new attacker crosses a threshold: GLM 5.3 in Claude Code already gets an exploit past Sonnet 5 in 17% of its attack slots.

title: Is the arXiv Apocalypse upon us? A break in preprint growth coincident with agentic AI
abstract: As an experiment in agentic assisted analysis, we used an agentic AI model to analyse the effect of agentic AI on arXiv submissions; data acquisition, analysis and the first draft were carried out by the model under the author's direction. Monthly arXiv submissions have grown exponentially for three decades, at about $9\%$ per year. Fitting a piecewise log-linear trend with seasonal modulation to the full record, we find two post-pandemic breaks in growth rate. The first, in mid-2022, precedes ChatGPT and is carried by the expansion of AI research within computer science (CS); outside CS, growth from 2022 to 2025 remained at $8\%$ per year. The second, between December 2025 and February 2026, follows the release of models capable of extended autonomous work and is absent from the AI categories themselves. Since December 2025 submissions without a CS listing have run $17\%$ above trend, and in September 2026 total submissions reached a record $40\,363$. The excess is largest in mathematics, where submissions doubled within a year, and follows a gradient from formal and theoretical fields to experimental ones that is not ordered by surveyed rates of AI-tool adoption. In mathematics the increase is distributed across subfields and authors, two-thirds of it arising from a larger number of distinct authors rather than from a few prolific submitters. Across fields the clearest signature is a shift to single authorship: solo-authored papers rose by $70\%$ within a year in mathematics and condensed matter, and by $44\%$ in quantitative biology even as its total output fell, but not in experimental particle physics. The analysis is deliberately agnostic of LLM-detection methods: it uses only submission counts and metadata, with treatment timing fixed by calendar dates, and is therefore free of the outcome-triggered timing bias of author-level studies.

title: py-ARGOS: A Python package for automatic, statistically principled discovery of ordinary differential equations from data
abstract: Recovering the governing equations of a dynamical system from data is a central problem in data-driven science, yet the available Python tooling forces a compromise among automation, statistical rigor, and reliability. We present py-ARGOS, a Python package implementing two automatic algorithms, bootstrap ARGOS and Bayesian-ARGOS, behind a uniform interface. Both are statistically principled throughout: automated model selection reduces the candidate library, each coefficient is reported with a bootstrap confidence or Bayesian credible interval that quantifies its uncertainty, and a term is retained when this interval excludes zero. Built-in diagnostics additionally flag unreliable fits. On chaotic benchmark systems, the two algorithms improve on the SINDy family's identification performance.

title: A Multi-Domain Study on the Effectiveness of LLMs at Writing Property-Based Tests
abstract: A property-based test (PBT) checks a property of a program on many generated inputs, but writing one takes a property, a generator of valid inputs, and an oracle. LLM-based PBT writers produce all three, yet they have been evaluated only on Python libraries. We study how two of them, Proptest-AI and Agentic-PBT, generalize to ten programs in five domains: deep learning libraries, databases, system software, compilers, and LLM serving engines. Most of these programs take text in their own language, such as queries, configurations, and programs. Agentic-PBT covers more branches than Proptest-AI on seven of the ten programs with Opus 5 and on all ten with GLM-5.3-Flash. Domain-specific fuzzers cover more of the compilers and of PostgreSQL and less of PyTorch than Agentic-PBT. We filed 180 bug reports, 44 of which duplicate reports that others filed after the models' knowledge cutoffs; maintainers have confirmed 65 of the others, in all five domains, and fixed 23. We draw lessons for building and evaluating such writers: low observability hurts them, and mature fuzzers paired with LLM-written properties could check that each feature behaves as documented.
