It supports benchmark calculations for user-specified parameter points, random and grid-based parameter scans, Markov-chain Monte Carlo exploration, comparisons with experimental limits, and publication-ready two- and three-dimensional visualizations. We describe the agent architecture, demonstrate its capabilities through representative benchmark calculations and regression tests, and discuss its current physics scope.

title: Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
abstract: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

title: RSI Arena: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement with Human Feedback
abstract: Can AI agents autonomously train useful language models and improve them using feedback from users? We introduce RSI Arena, a two-stage study of autonomous post-training as a step toward recursive self-improvement. Ten frontier models act as training agents, each starting from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B Base. During a six-day first stage, each agent has 1,000 GPU-hours and $300 in API credit on a shared 64-GPU cluster, independently selecting data, implementing training procedures, and choosing checkpoints. We evaluate their models on 20 benchmarks and through blind human evaluations. All ten agents produce working assistants, with the strongest model, trained by GPT-6 Astra, closing a median of 76% of the base-to-Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks. Its human-preference rating is also close to NVIDIA Instruct after statistical adjustment for answer length and formatting. In Stage 2, each agent receives the comparison records and votes involving its Stage 1 model and is given three additional days for further training. Using NVIDIA Instruct as a common reference across the two evaluation rounds, we observe an improvement from Stage 1 to Stage 2 in the style-adjusted relative rating of eight of the ten models. We show that benchmark gains were modest, with no clear link to preference gains, while some agents encouraged longer responses and one model showed increased harmful compliance on StrongREJECT. RSI Arena provides an auditable setting for studying how human feedback can guide autonomous model development. It takes a step toward recursive self-improvement with human feedback (RSIHF), in which people help define what improvement means for the AI systems they use.

title: PreView: Enhancing GUI Grounding with Preprocessed Views and Cues
abstract: GUI grounding requires locating small controls in cluttered screenshots and identifying which control a natural-language instruction refers to. Cropping and enlargement can expose local detail, but the resulting image may still leave ambiguity about the intended target. We propose PreView, an auxiliary preprocessor that improves the inputs to an existing grounding model without further training that model. PreView prepares two complementary types of input features: task-relevant views for localization and candidate-specific cues for target understanding. A trained lightweight auxiliary model predicts and refines a center, crops the screenshot into a local view, and enlarges that view for zoomed-in grounding. It also prepares a visual cue (i.e., a red-circle marker with a location hint) and a textual cue describing the candidate's identity or function. The frozen grounding model uses the prepared inputs to predict the final click. Across five benchmarks, PreView improves the average grounding accuracy of Qwen3-VL-2B, OS-Atlas-4B, and Qwen3-VL-4B without further training these grounding models. Extensive analyses examine the contributions of views and cues, center refinement, and visual input budgets.

title: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
abstract: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.

title: Fractional reversible chemical kinetics: Time-Driven Monte Carlo method and application to enzyme conformational dynamics
abstract: In this work, we present a fractional framework for reversible two-state chemical kinetics derived from the Continuous-Time Random Walk (CTRW) formalism with Mittag-Leffler waiting-time distributions. This derivation provides a microscopic basis for the fractional kinetic equations governed by the Caputo derivative. An exact analytical solution is obtained, yielding closed-form expressions for the time evolution of the state populations. To the best of our knowledge, a time-driven Monte Carlo algorithm is developed for the first time to simulate the irreversible underlying non-Markovian stochastic dynamics governed by a system of Caputo fractional differential equations. The proposed framework is applied to the conformational dynamics of the TbQSOX enzyme, whose relaxation exhibits power-law behavior. The fractional model accurately reproduces the experimental kinetics, providing an estimate of the fractional order $α= 0.22$, which is consistent with the observed anomalous dynamics.

title: Beyond Affine Reconstruction: Multi-Resolution Transformer DeepONets for the Radiative Transfer Equation
abstract: Radiative heat transfer plays a dominant role in fire simulations, where solving the radiative transfer equation (RTE) is a computational bottleneck. Neural operators can accelerate these computations by learning solution operators from offline simulation data. However, conventional DeepONet surrogates rely on fixed-grid inputs and affine reconstruction, limiting their flexibility across resolutions and their approximation accuracy at a fixed latent dimension. In this paper, we develop a transformer-based DeepONet for multi-resolution RTE surrogate modelling. The proposed approach combines a Perceiver encoder, which maps temperature and absorption coefficient fields at different spatial resolutions into a fixed-size latent representation, with a cross-attention decoder that enables non-affine reconstruction of the radiative intensity. This architecture allows a single model to process inputs at varying resolutions without resampling them onto a common grid. We formulate a computable empirical version of a previously derived theoretical lower bound for affine reconstruction, enabling direct comparison with model errors on the same dataset. Experiments on a two-dimensional pool-fire dataset demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms autoencoder-based DeepONets in predicting both radiative intensity and incident radiation, with fewer trainable parameters. Power spectral density analysis shows improved preservation of small-scale structures. Both affine baselines remain above the corresponding lower bound at all evaluated ranks, whereas the proposed model achieves a training error below it at one matched latent dimension, demonstrating the potential of non-affine reconstruction to overcome this representational limitation. Experiments on a dataset combining three spatial resolutions confirm the accuracy advantage of the approach at each input resolution.

title: Energy-Based Fault Detection and Isolation Framework for Flat Port-Hamiltonian Mechanical Systems
abstract: Fault diagnosis during regulated motion requires informative signals even when feedback attenuates tracking deviations. This paper develops an energy-based diagnostic framework that constructs mechanical port-power residuals without a dedicated dynamic observer. Spectral Hamiltonian Algebraic Power Evaluation (SHAPE) combines port-Hamiltonian variables and differential flatness to generate nominal power references from planned motion for fully actuated mechanical systems with collocated actuation. Subtracting these references from commanded effort multiplied by measured flow yields residuals whose final evaluation requires neither recursive observer updates nor measured-state dynamics calculations. Continuous wavelet transform (CWT) scalograms and a shared-encoder convolutional neural network are used to distinguish nominal operation, actuator loss of effectiveness, anomalous friction, and vibration from complete trajectories. Evaluation uses a simulated six degree of freedom Kinova manipulator under model predictive control and fixed plant-model mismatch, with single faults at a specified joint. Across five training seeds and 3000 held-out test runs, SHAPE-CWT achieves a mean accuracy of 84.69 percent, versus 81.67 percent for torque residuals and 97.17 percent for the generalized momentum observer under common CWT processing. The respective sample standard deviations are 0.70, 0.70, and 0.37 percentage points. These results demonstrate useful fault-type discrimination from algebraic power residuals, while severity-excitation profiles and offline velocity perturbations reveal limits to their diagnostic capability.

title: Seeing the Options: Typed Decisions over Visual Candidates with Reusable Option Memory
abstract: Agents end many steps in a typed decision over a set of candidates: which screen element to click, which product to pick. System One models answer in one forward pass, and Jeva showed that four properties the setting demands - a "none of the above" probability, invariance to candidate order, scalability in the number of candidates, and reuse of candidate computation - follow from encoding the request and each candidate separately and letting a request state read a candidate memory. Jeva is text-only, and existing multimodal System One models (OneJev, Jev-Omni) put images in the request while candidates stay text in letter slots. This paper asks what happens to the four properties, and to accuracy, when the candidates themselves are images. Iris admits image, text, or mixed candidates and leaves Jeva's decision module untouched. On a visual-candidate benchmark built from Multimodal-Mind2Web (every candidate is the element's screenshot crop, K=16, three splits), independent encoding reaches 78.4/72.1/74.8% with a flip rate of exactly zero, while joint encoding (OneJev-4B fine-tuned on the same data) reaches 90.6/89.5/91.6% but changes its answer on 8-10% of records when the crops are reordered. Most of the gap is the candidate not seeing the request: a third design that encodes each candidate after the state - but never after another candidate - keeps order invariance exactly, shares the state pass through a forked cache, and reaches 92.1/87.0/90.2% at a third of OneJev's latency with a calibrated null probability (AUROC 0.93-0.97). Letting pooled candidates see each other (set attention, token-level reads, multi-vector memory) buys nothing, because the encoder maps visually distinct elements to vectors within cosine 0.999 of each other. Reusing image candidates across requests cuts latency 37x at K=256 and 191x at K=2048. Code: https://github.com/lllfx/Iris

title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws
abstract: This work develops a differentiable finite element framework based on an intrinsic cohesive-zone formulation for identifying traction-separation laws from global force-displacement histories and spatially sparse strain measurements. The framework employs physics-constrained neural networks to represent flexible, thermodynamically structured cohesive laws, with sensitivities computed through automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for the history-dependent evolution of interfacial damage. To enable identification of spatially heterogeneous cohesive behavior, we extend learned constitutive priors to irreversible interfacial damage by constructing a shared, low-dimensional family of cohesive laws from representative traction-separation histories. This representation exploits common constitutive structure and parameter sharing to reduce the number of unknowns and regularize the inverse problem, while allowing local cohesive behavior to vary spatially through latent coordinates. Numerical investigations involving double-cantilever beams and fiber-matrix composites demonstrate that accurate reproduction of global force-displacement responses does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying cohesive laws. Incorporating spatially resolved strain measurements substantially improves constitutive identification, even when the admissible responses are constrained by a learned prior. Comparisons with conventional bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization further illustrate the benefits of the learned constitutive representation and adjoint-based identification for high-dimensional inverse problems.

title: Projection-Based Federated Learning on Compact Submanifolds with Geometry-Independent Differential Privacy
abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model across clients without exchanging their data, yet the updates they transmit still leak information about individual records. Enforcing differential privacy is harder still when the model parameters lie on a Riemannian manifold. Existing methods rebuild the noise added for privacy in the geometry of each new iterate, aggregate through intrinsic maps that often lack a closed form, and prove convergence only in restricted regimes. We introduce DP-RFedProj, a record-level differentially private federated learning method for compact submanifolds that aggregates through closed-form projections and privatises gradients in a fixed ambient geometry. Each client may run any stochastic first-order optimiser, take several local steps, and participate only intermittently. An explicit record-level $f$-DP guarantee holds for the entire training transcript, independently of the manifold, the aggregation scheme and the local optimiser. We establish convergence of DP-RFedProj when each client runs Riemannian SGD locally and the server aggregates by projected averaging, and show that privacy enters the rate through a term scaling with the manifold's intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient one. Synthetic experiments on federated PCA over the Grassmann manifold corroborate these findings. On EEG motor-imagery classification with SPDNet, whose weights lie on the Stiefel manifold, the method outperforms a Euclidean baseline at every privacy budget considered. In both experimental settings, our accounting requires five to six times less noise than that of the closest prior method for the same budget, which translates into higher utility.

title: RoboJev: An Open Vision-Language Judge for Robot Success Detection
abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.

title: Task-Directed Spectral Design for Local Quantum Tomography
abstract: Many tomography tasks require only a low-dimensional function of the state. We study local pure-state tomography under projective-fidelity access when a parametric model, a credible center, and a differentiable downstream task are known before acquisition. The pullback Fubini--Study metric and the task metric define coordinate-invariant generalized eigendirections, which we realize as a fixed library of geodesic fidelity probes. We prove two optimality results: the probe aligned with a task coordinate is its unique variance-minimizing location up to orientation, and, when prior and measurement information are diagonal in this basis, a diminishing-return greedy rule exactly minimizes the integer-budget local task-variance surrogate over the spectral library. Under common per-shot information and the stated large-budget condition, the absolute and relative gaps to arbitrary probe directions are respectively \(O(B^{-3})\) and \(O(B^{-2})\). A closed-form local estimator is followed by a task-metric localization projection that cannot increase quadratic task loss when localization holds. In six-qubit numerical experiments, the Schmidt-spectrum design activates only one or two settings and has lower mean task error than the post hoc best adaptive results across all tested dimensions and copy budgets. For full-state tomography, it likewise has lower mean infidelity throughout the tested local regime. The fixed batch uses no feedback loops and far fewer settings; under the illustrative latency model, its acquisition cost is roughly three to four orders of magnitude lower than that of the adaptive methods.

title: Ring-0 by Default: Agents as Operating Systems (AaOS)
abstract: LLM agents now read and write files, start processes and subagents, fetch network content, load third-party extensions, and save and resume state, which are the responsibilities of an operating system. They gained these functions within about three years, but not the protections that operating systems built over five decades: whatever the model outputs, whether it follows the user, a tool result, or a downloaded skill, runs with the full authority of the host user, in effect at ring 0. Prior work builds an operating system for agents (OS4A); we argue that a deployed agent already is like an operating system (AaOS) and analyze it as one. Taking the mechanisms of standard OS textbooks as a checklist, we map 116 mechanisms in 19 subsystems to their agent counterparts, from product documentation, source code, and the literature, and label each as isomorphic, degraded (function present, protection dependent on the model), missing, mutated, or novel. Only 11 are isomorphic and 65 are missing, most of them protections: privilege separation, resource quotas, transactions, and tamper-proof audit. Existing defenses confine the whole agent or review its extensions and leave this interior unprotected, and by Anderson's reference-monitor criteria (non-bypassable, tamper-proof, verifiable), rules written in the prompt satisfy none. We test the map with thirteen experiments on Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI, covering 25 mechanisms whose enforcement documentation cannot settle: 16 match the analysis, 7 gain a more precise description, and 2 change verdict. Checks sit in single tools, so the shell bypasses them; all three CLIs load forged transcript records on resume; and task control, sub-agent permissions, and model-based monitors are weak. We identify five problems for which no OS defense transfers and derive a prioritized list of open problems from the gaps of the map.

title: Inverse problems with fractional operators: an analytical study and its numerical linear algebra treatment via the GLT theory
abstract: Fractional derivatives model memory effects and nonlocal interactions beyond classical integer-order models. Fractional differential equations (FDEs) thus describe anomalous diffusion, transport in heterogeneous media, and hereditary dynamics. Their nonlocality, however, makes inverse problems challenging: unknown sources, coefficients, or initial conditions must be recovered from indirect and noisy data. Inverse problems for FDEs are usually ill-posed in the Hadamard sense, so regularization, such as the quasi-boundary value method, is required for stable reconstruction. Discretization produces large linear systems whose matrices inherit the nonlocal structure of fractional operators. Understanding the asymptotic spectral properties of these matrix sequences is essential for efficient solvers and preconditioners. Generalized Locally Toeplitz (GLT) theory provides a unified framework for the spectral distribution of large structured matrices and for preconditioner design. This thesis uses GLT theory to analyze matrix sequences from inverse problems for FDEs, construct structure-preserving preconditioners, and study nonlinear operations in the GLT algebra. In particular, it proves maximal distribution results for geometric means of GLT sequences: when the symbols commute, the geometric mean sequence remains GLT without symbol invertibility. This resolves a long-standing conjecture and shows maximality in the noncommuting degenerate case. Overall, the thesis integrates regularization, spectral analysis, and preconditioning into a coherent computational framework for inverse problems in nonlocal fractional dynamics, while enriching structured matrix analysis.

title: CFL-aware edge design for graph neural solvers of hyperbolic transport
abstract: Hyperbolic partial differential equations (PDEs) transport information at finite speed along characteristics, often producing shocks and discontinuities that are challenging to capture numerically. Graph neural networks (GNNs) offer learned update rules, but neighbor aggregation alone does not tell a GNN how far information must travel and along which edge. As a result, when a GNN model takes a time step larger than what was used in training, shock fronts smear and oscillations grow. In this work, we ask whether making the scale of transport explicit as an edge-local Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) signal can enhance GNNs' ability to model hyperbolic PDEs. Holding the architecture fixed, we vary only the information given to each edge, from a raw edge form to forms that progressively expose the edge-local transport interaction through direction, length, and wave speed. Because all of these are computed from the same ingredients, what changes is not the amount of information but its form. The results show a consistent pattern, in which feature count is not the limiting factor, and appending CFL directly to a raw edge form produces almost no benefit. The CFL conditioning proves most effective when the edge information already exposes the transport interaction, reducing final-step error by 10.4-14.4%, and the improvement widens as the step size grows larger. Notably, this improvement arises not from smearing the solution but from suppressing oscillations near shocks. These results point to a specific design principle that CFL conditioning is most effective when the edge representation already separates the direction of interaction from spatial scale, so that the CFL value has a well-defined quantity to modulate.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to System 1 Models: Fast Decision-Making Beyond LLMS
abstract: Large Language Models excel at reasoning and generation but their autoregressive, token-by-token inference makes them unnecessarily slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated for the many routine decisions (routing, gating, scoring, classification) that modern AI systems require at sub-second latency. A growing class of models addresses this gap: System 1 decision models, architectures that map an input directly to a typed, structured decision in a single forward pass. This guide provides a comprehensive, practitioner-oriented treatment of the field. We propose a five-family taxonomy covering encoder-based classifiers, reward models, non-autoregressive decision engines, contrastive decision models, and extraction models, and we provide in-depth coverage of each family's architecture, training methodology, and deployment trade-offs. A central theme is calibration: we develop the theory of proper scoring rules, analyze Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), and examine recently discovered phenomena including IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift. On the integration side, we describe how System 1 models serve as decision infrastructure within agentic workflows and System 1 + System 2 cascades that route between fast and slow models based on calibrated confidence. The guide covers 18 application domains, maps the rapidly growing open-source ecosystem (over 70 model reproductions in weeks), provides runnable code throughout, and includes a practitioner's checklist, an open-source model zoo, and 22 self-assessment questions with detailed answers. Spanning 190 references, it is intended as a unified entry point for researchers and engineers working at the intersection of fast decision-making, calibration, and production AI systems.

title: Unlocking the Specialization Capability of PPG Foundation Models for Wearable Signals through Structured Pruning and Adaptive Fine-Tuning
abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) plays a central role in wearable health monitoring and clinical decision support. However, existing approaches to universal PPG representation learning are predominantly trained on high-quality large-scale datasets obtained from oximeters in hospital settings and often struggle to adapt to sparse and low-quality real-world datasets, thereby limiting their generalization to clinically relevant tasks on prevalent PPG data such as collected from wearable devices. Surprisingly, even after full fine-tuning, PPG foundation models cannot consistently outperform general-purpose time-series models. Therefore, a key question is how to effectively adapt PPG foundation models to target prediction tasks. Through empirical studies on various PPG foundation models, we find that pretrained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and computational redundancy, suggesting that PPG foundation models have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures for different prediction tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning-and-fine-tuning framework, SPAFT, which regularizes the adaptive fine-tuning process by constraining it to a more relevant and compact parameter space based on parameter importance and structural redundancy. Extensive experiments across four PPG foundation models, five benchmark datasets, and ten downstream tasks demonstrate that SPAFT achieves win rates of 82.8% and 87.5% on regression and classification tasks, respectively. This prune-then-finetune paradigm often enables PPG foundation models to achieve state-of-the-art performance, laying a promising foundation for the real-world clinical deployment of PPG foundation models and the development of personalized PPG foundation models.

title: Data-Driven LQR with Uncertainty Refinement and Domain Randomization---Part~I: Certified Uncertainty Refinement
abstract: Learning controllers from trajectories corrupted by process and measurement noise is difficult when the system matrices and the noise covariances are unknown: noisy regressors bias least squares, and model uncertainty cannot be quantified without the noise covariance, which can only be estimated from residuals of the uncertain model. This paper, Part~I of a two-part study, resolves both obstacles with a finite-sample framework that certifies, and iteratively refines, uncertainty sets for the model, the noise in the collected data, and the noise covariance. A closed-loop parametrization based on delayed instrumental variables (IVs) removes the bias and assigns to every candidate model exactly one noise sequence that reproduces the data. Learning this noise breaks the circular dependence: the noise sequences give the covariance estimate directly, models whose noise violates the prior or the statistical certificates are discarded, and the surviving models yield a tighter covariance certificate. Several delayed instruments further tighten the model set and give a certified test of data consistency. We prove finite-sample containment of the true model, noise, and covariance, recursive nesting, and convergence at the IV rate. Part~II uses these certificates for domain-randomized linear quadratic regulator synthesis.

title: EdgeDeID: A 0.6B Clinical De-identifier Trained Without Real Patient Data
abstract: De-identifying clinical notes with a hosted language model discloses the information the step is meant to protect. We present EdgeDeID, a 0.6B-parameter decoder-only de-identifier that runs locally and is trained without real patient text: three LLM teachers write synthetic notes, a single labeler re-annotates them into one convention, and the model learns to emit a typed XML schema of the identifiers it finds. On a 100-note synthetic in-domain benchmark with manually verified annotations it reaches 0.994 micro-F1 and leaves no missed identifier in 99% of notes, against 0.857 and 12% for the strongest of eight off-the-shelf systems. Quantized, it runs on CPU in 615 MB. Of three additions to supervised training, only a verifier adapter helps: it separates complete from incomplete outputs of other systems at 0.94 AUROC, whereas reinforcement learning with a recall-weighted reward and a rule-based post-processing layer leave in-domain results unchanged. On MIMIC ICU nursing notes F1 falls to 0.48. The errors follow two properties our synthetic notes lack, telegraphic style and low identifier density, and three hand-written in-context examples recover 0.08 F1 without annotated target data.

title: Build, Don't Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players
abstract: Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AutoTavern, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AutoTavern built TavernGym, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TavernAgent, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TavernAgent plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard's measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server's ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TavernBench, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TavernAgent answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TavernBench and TavernGym at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern.

title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
abstract: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.

title: ReGE: Stronger Agents through Experience Synthesis
abstract: Repeated attempts at interactive tasks uncover facts, useful operations, and failures that can inform subsequent execution. We introduce ReGE, a framework for turning this recorded experience into guidance for a fresh attempt. Its main implementation, ReGE-Syn, uses a single coach call to jointly synthesize bounded execution records and available artifacts into self-contained guidance, connecting task-specific findings with proposed actions and relevant pitfalls. A student starts from the task's initial environment state and adapts this guidance to current observations. Source generation, synthesis, and student execution use the same base model, without parameter updates or a stronger teacher. Across four benchmarks, ReGE improves accuracy by an average of 9.9 percentage points for GPT and 8.8 percentage points for Claude compared with unguided execution. On matched BrowseComp-Plus subsets, ReGE-Syn reduces guidance-construction tokens by 98.2\% on GPT and 95.5\% on Claude relative to adapted AggAgent, with observed success. Combined construction and execution tokens decrease by 15.7\% and 35.4\%, respectively, counting input plus output and excluding source generation. BrowseComp-Plus ablations further associate access to process information with fewer student steps and show that joint synthesis produces substantially shorter guidance than Direct history or Independent summaries, with observed success. These results demonstrate how agents can use their own recorded experience to improve subsequent task completion, and suggest a low-cost way to consolidate the execution records of parallel agent systems such as agent swarms.

title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents
abstract: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.

title: The Computational Assessment Stack: An Architecture for AI-Native Measurement
abstract: Test development is shifting toward automation and agentic artificial intelligence (AI), in which autonomous systems draft items at scale, assemble test forms, administer adaptive assessments, score complex responses, and monitor test quality. As autonomous systems take on more of this work, the architecture underlying test development must change to preserve assessment quality under the new paradigm. This paper proposes the Computational Assessment Stack (CAS), a four-layer architecture for AI-native measurement where every stage of the assessment lifecycle shares a unifying computational construct representation as its base layer. This representation is a machine-readable, modular, and versioned knowledge graph. Three layers are built above it: computational content generation that builds on the knowledge graph; computational psychometrics that derives substantive structure directly from the knowledge graph; an orchestration layer in which agentic systems operationalize the stack under human governance. The paper's core contribution is architectural. Building on foundational psychometric frameworks, the CAS provides a persistent representation that unifies the four layers. Unlike the descriptive prose traditionally used to define constructs in test development, the proposed architecture renders measurement assumptions inspectable and their consequences empirically testable.

title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology
abstract: Reduced-order models simplify fluid simulation by representing complex flows with a small number of spatial modes. Building on Laplacian Eigenfluids, we introduce Neural Eigenfluid Bases (NEB), a neural representation whose basis functions can be evaluated anywhere in space. We enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries directly through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions. Geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization then learn an ordered basis. We connect learning in potential and velocity spaces, and derive a spectral-variance relation explaining why these objectives weight approximate modes differently, even though their exact positive spectra agree. Gauge fixing reduces the number of spatial derivatives needed for potential learning, while a Dirichlet energy loss learns independent circulation fields around obstacles. With 1024 modes, both objectives keep velocity errors below 1% in periodic vortex merger. For random flows around obstacles, potential-based learning captures more initial energy and gives lower final errors than numerical Laplacian bases of the same size. The reduced state is about a thousand times smaller than the full reference model. Three-dimensional tests separate spatial reconstruction errors from errors in coefficient evolution. Precomputed Galerkin operators allow millisecond-scale updates when the same basis is reused across simulations. This provides a physically constrained basis for continuous flow reconstruction and efficient reduced-order simulation.

title: O Mirror, Where Art Thou?
abstract: Wavefront sensing reveals that a telescope is misaligned, but not which mirror moved or by how much; inferring the mirror positions themselves turns alignment into a direct correction. We describe a simulation framework for inferring telescope mirror misalignment from multi-field Point Spread Function (PSF) measurements projected onto Circular-Bessel and Zernike basis vectors. Two case studies are presented: a Hubble Space Telescope model with five secondary-mirror degrees of freedom and a three-mirror anastigmat with ten primary and secondary mirror degrees of freedom. In both cases, field-dependent multivariate Gaussian likelihoods are explored with nested sampling and refined with differential evolution. Recovered states are validated with residual PSF images and optical path difference (OPD) measurements. In the Hubble benchmark, differential evolution recovers injected misalignments to less than 0.01 microns and reduces on-axis OPD error from 2.3 waves to 3 x 10E-8 waves. In the TMA study, the posterior shows broad marginals and correlated parameter pairs that suggest partial degeneracies at higher dimension; differential evolution recovers the truth alignment state less precisely than in the Hubble benchmark (less than 17 microns) and reduces on-axis OPD error from 8.24 waves to 2 x 10E-3 waves. This generalizable algorithm enables direct sensing of the state of an optical system and automated alignment.

title: Exploring Students’ Perceptions of an Asynchronous Oral Communication Course
abstract: The purpose of the study was to describe undergraduate students’ perceptions of an asynchronous oral communication course taught in a college of agriculture in hopes of gaining an increased understanding of how the educational experience can be improved and inform future asynchronous teaching practices. This qualitative study utilized individual, semi-structured interviews (n = 16) to explore students’ perceptions of an asynchronous oral communication course. Data were analyzed using domain analysis and four domains emerged: (a) decision to enroll, (b) quality indicators, (c) learning outcomes, and (d) limitations. Overall, participants were satisfied with their learning experience and believe their oral communication skills improved. In addition, participants perceived they were more skilled in utilizing technology for speaking in digital contexts. Therefore, we recommend the asynchronous oral communication course continue to be offered. Also, because of the increasing need to effectively communicate in digital contexts, colleges of agriculture should consider if there is a need to offer an oral communication course specific to digital contexts. Future research should determine curricular needs related to digital contexts and continue to investigate the efficacy of asynchronous oral communication courses seeking to replicate an in-person oral communication course.

title: From naïve to vigilant: how inflammatory and metabolic cues shape human T cells
abstract: CD4⁺ T cells are essential regulators of adaptive immunity and can differentiate into distinct helper T cell subsets depending on signals from their environment. Among these subsets, T helper 17 (Th17) cells play a crucial role in protecting against bacterial and fungal infections but are also implicated in chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. This thesis investigates how environmental and metabolic factors influence human Th17 cell differentiation and function. Using a defined human in vitro model, we demonstrate that Th17 development is shaped by a combination of signals, including TGF-β, extracellular lactate, and hypoxia. These factors modify cellular transcriptional programs and converge on key regulatory pathways, particularly STAT3. We further show that mitochondrial activity is closely linked to Th17 differentiation. Cells with high mitochondrial membrane potential are more likely to develop into Th17 cells, but also display characteristics associated with functional exhaustion. The clinical relevance of these findings was explored in osteoarthritis, where synovial T cells were found to remain activated and responsive despite longstanding disease. Together, the results show that T cell differentiation is highly dynamic and determined by interactions between environmental cues, metabolism, and tissue context. Understanding these interactions may provide new therapeutic opportunities for chronic inflammatory diseases.

title: Gis and Artificial Intelligence-based Forecasting of Regional Sustainable Development
abstract: Ensuring the sustainable development of the regional economy has become the most important issue on a global scale. In 2024-2026, growth rates in the countries that account for more than 80% of the world's population and global GDP remain below those of the decade preceding the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2025, the German geospatial analytics (Geospatial Analytics) market is valued at USD 1.45 billion, and it is expected to reach USD 2.55 billion by 2030. Therefore, using GIS technologies as a lever for forecasting regions, and studying their structural components and their impact on the formation of regional economic policy, is a pressing scientific problem.

title: A Research Study on Effects of Technology in the Banking Sector on Customer Services at Pallakkad
abstract: The rapid evolution of financial technology (FinTech) has fundamentally redefined the operational paradigms of the banking sector, shifting traditional brick-and-mortar operations toward digital self-service ecosystems. This empirical study investigates the impact of banking technology—including Automated Teller Machines (ATMs), Internet Banking, Mobile Banking applications, Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and automated kiosk services—on customer service delivery and satisfaction across Palakkad district, Kerala. Recognized as a unique blend of semi-urban commercial centers and extensive agricultural/rural belts, Palakkad presents a diverse demographic landscape for studying digital banking adoption. The primary objective of this research is to evaluate how technological integration influences core service quality dimensions, namely responsiveness, reliability, accessibility, transaction speed, and security. Concurrently, the study examines the operational challenges faced by non-digital natives, including network downtime, digital security anxieties, hidden transactional charges, and the loss of personal human touch. Utilizing a descriptive and analytical research design, primary quantitative data was collected from a stratified random sample of 200 bank customers across both public and private sector banks in Palakkad municipal and surrounding rural areas. Statistical techniques including simple percentage analysis, Chi-square tests, and Likert scale mean satisfaction scoring—were applied to assess customer attitudes and usage patterns. Based on these empirical insights, the paper provides actionable strategies to foster financial inclusion and optimize digital service delivery throughout Palakkad's banking ecosystem.

title: Do Electricity Transmission and Distribution Losses Predict Economic Performance? Evidence from Pakistan’s Output and Capital Formation, 1990–2023
abstract: Pakistan’s power-sector debate often treats electricity transmission and distribution (T&D) losses as if they were a direct measure of unreliable service. That equivalence is economically problematic: the annual loss ratio mixes physical and commercial losses and does not observe the timing or duration of firms’ power interruptions. This study examines a narrower, testable proposition—whether annual changes in Pakistan’s national T&D-loss ratio improve predictions of subsequent real output and fixed-capital-formation growth. We assemble direct, full-precision World Development Indicators (WDI/IEA) loss observations and supporting WDI macroeconomic series for 1990–2023, then estimate parsimonious dynamic growth equations over 1992–2023 (32 annual observations). Newey–West HAC inference yields coefficients of −0.163 percentage points for real GDP-per-capita growth (95% CI −0.446 to 0.120; p = 0.247) and 0.111 percentage points for real fixed-investment-per-capita growth (95% CI −0.853 to 1.075; p = 0.815) per percentage-point increase in lagged annual losses. Neither association is statistically precise. Alternative specifications, influence checks and a 12-year recursive forecast comparison do not establish robust incremental predictive value: including the grid-loss change increases GDP-growth forecast RMSE from 1.980 to 2.053 percentage points. The article contributes a primary-source-audited test of an often-conflated electricity indicator and explains why null aggregate predictive evidence should not be interpreted as evidence that outages are harmless. The policy implication is to evaluate network loss recovery and actual supply reliability with separate performance measures.
journal: International Journal of Business and Management Sciences

title: Estimating healthcare cost savings from greenspace in Washington
abstract: Greenspace is increasingly recognized as public-health infrastructure, yet its potential contribution to healthcare cost savings remains poorly quantified beyond a relatively small number of studies. To contribute to these investigations, we estimated potential avoided healthcare expenditures associated with residential greenness in Washington using a benefit-transfer framework. We applied decile-specific relative healthcare-cost ratios from a Northern California cohort of approximately five million Kaiser Permanente members to population-weighted distributions of satellite-derived normalized difference vegetation index across Washington census block groups. Ratios were calibrated to Washingtons 2020 statewide per-capita healthcare expenditure, allowing estimates to reflect the states own cost baseline. Estimated annual per-capita costs declined from $6,472.75 in the least-green decile to $5,939.39 in the greenest, a difference of $533.35. Simulated interventions yielded estimated annual statewide savings of $45.6 million from raising the lowest decile to the next decile, $157.7 million from lifting the four lowest deciles to Decile five, and $56.9 million from urban-core greening in Washingtons five largest cities. These estimates are modeled associations, not causal forecasts, and depend on transferability between regional populations and on normalized difference vegetation index as an incomplete proxy for meaningful nature access. Nonetheless, the findings highlight increased and equitable greening efforts as a potentially consequential component of preventive health and infrastructure policy.

title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75-0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66-0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

title: Death of the Author, Birth of the Algorithm? Reimagining Literary Meaning- Making in the Age of Generative AI
abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced new possibilities for literary interpretation, challenging traditional assumptions about authorship, readership and textual meaning. While Roland Barthes’ concept of the “Death of the Author” displaced authorial intention as the primary source of meaning, contemporary AI technologies raise questions about whether algorithms are becoming active participants in interpretive processes. This study explores how generative AI reshapes literary meaning- making and examines the implications of AI- generated interpretations for literary studies in the digital age. This qualitative exploratory study was conducted among 20 undergraduate students enrolled in a BA English programme at a private university in Sri Lanka. Drawing on Barthes’ notion of the Death of the Author, Michael Foucault’s concept of the author function, and reader- response theories advanced by Wolfgang Iser and Stanley Fish, the study critically examines the role of generative AI in the production and mediation of literary interpretations. Relevant scholarly literature on AI- assisted reading and digital textuality is analysed to develop a theoretical framework for understanding algorithmic participation in literary meaning- making. The analysis suggest that generative AI complicates traditional distinctions between author, reader, and text. Rather than functioning as an author in the conventional sense, AI appears to operate as an interpretive agent capable of generating multiple readings based on patterns derived from vast textual corpora. This development extends reader- centred approaches to literary interpretation while simultaneously raising concerns regarding originality, authority, and the pedagogical use of AI-generated analyses. The study argues that AI- generated interpretations should be viewed not as replacements for human reading but as additional voices within broader interpretive communities. The paper proposes that literary studies must reconsider established theories of authorship and interpretation in response to emerging AI technologies. By positioning AI as a participant in, rather than a determinant of, meaning- making, the study contributes to ongoing discussions in literary theory, semiotics, and digital humanities. The findings offer insights for educators, researchers, and students navigating literary interpretation in increasingly AI- mediated learning environments.
journal: Proceedings of the Annual International Research Symposium 2026, Sri Palee Campus, University of Colombo

title: Transformation of the Kohombayo Folk Belief: A Study on Daduru Oya Valley in Sri Lanka
abstract: The belief in Kohombayo is an ancient folklore tradition associated with paddy cultivation. The Kohombayo were believed to be invisible beings who steal a portion of harvest, a series of ritualistic practices were performed at threshing floor to prevent loss. This research aims to identify history of Kohombayo belief, rituals associated with them, and how modern farming methods have influenced this. Drawing on Walter Benjamin’s theory of mechanical and digital reproduction, this study explores, how agriculture modernization and digitalization have transformed to influence of this belief. The research was conducted through qualitative research methodology with Bandarigalgoda village in Daduru oya valley serving as study area. Data were collected from 55 residents through non participant observation. Library study incorporated with books and research articles, field study incorporated with interviews and questionnaires. Thematic analysis was adopted to interpret. Findings reveal that, while the Kohombayo belief and rituals like spilling milk, hiding salt in threshing floor, drawing symbol called Alu yantharaya on threshing floor to prevent harvest from Kohombayo , is largely declined due to introduction of machine harvesting, it has not completely vanished. Only four adult participants were familiar with term Kohombayo and limited knowledge was preserved, mainly among the oldest generation. They still maintain Kohombayo faith in belief, communicate through dreams, practicing divine remembrance while offering alms and planting Kohombo trees, as symbolic acts of protection for their harvest. The study concludes that the last bearers of Kohombayo knowledge are fading with rise of the digital era, as younger generation increasingly rely on technological and digital knowledge rather than traditional beliefs. Preserving vanishing folk heritage must be prioritized before it is lost to modern agriculture and digital influences.

title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

title: Human Agents in the Loop
Improvement of DSSAT CSM‐CROPGRO‐Cotton model for response to water, nitrogen, weather, and management
abstract: The goal of this study was to update the CSM‐CROPGRO‐Cotton model for its ability to simulate cotton ( Gossypium hirsutum L.) lint yield and cardinal temperature effects on physiological processes, followed by a thorough recalibration against extensive data on seed‐cotton yield, lint yield and percentage, crop mass, and time series growth data collected on 11 cotton cultivars in 143 treatments over 21 site‐years in Arizona, Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina (where CSM is Cropping System Model). Model parameters were updated for seed‐cotton composition, cardinal temperatures for critical processes, and dependency of lint percentage on temperature, drought and N stress, and cultivar. The D ‐statistic for time series variables averaged over all site treatments was 0.947, 0.977, 0.896, 0.865, 0.937, 0.978, 0.955, and 0.974 for canopy height, total crop mass, leaf area index, leaf mass, stem mass, boll mass, boll harvest index, and vegetative stage, respectively. Additional data from 46 treatments in 10 site‐years in Mississippi were used for calibrating lint yield and percentage. For these treatments, relative root mean square error (RRMSE) was 16.5%, 20.0%, 20.7%, and 2.7% for crop mass, seed‐cotton yield, lint yield, and percentage, while respective D ‐statistics were 0.871, 0.822, 0.786, and 0.795. For end‐of‐season outputs across treatments in all 31 site‐years of experiments, RRMSE was 14.5%, 25.9%, 22.4%, and 6.0% for crop mass, seed‐cotton yield, lint yield, and percentage, while respective D ‐statistics were 0.950, 0.925, 0.955, and 0.869. The model was successfully evaluated against lint yield and percentage for the 1999–2019 Arkansas cotton variety trials. The improved model, its parameters, and appropriate experimental files will be included in a future release of DSSAT (Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer).

title: Navigation-Guided Spatial Mapping of Subclinical Local Invasion in Sinonasal and Nasopharyngeal Malignancies.
abstract: BACKGROUND Subclinical local invasion (SLI) beyond radiologically evident margins poses a major challenge in the management of sinonasal and nasopharyngeal malignancies (SNNM). The biological behavior underlying this phenomenon remains poorly characterized, particularly regarding its spatial extent and histology-dependent patterns. METHODS This prospective study included patients undergoing surgical resection of SNNM with intraoperative surgical navigation (SN). Intraoperative biopsies were systematically mapped and spatially correlated with preoperative imaging. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated the association between positive biopsy probability, distance from the gross tumor surface, and histologic characteristics. RESULTS Fifty-four patients and 569 biopsies were analyzed; 78 (13.7%) were positive. A significant inverse association between distance from the gross tumor surface and positive biopsy probability was observed, with an approximately 5.1% reduction in odds per millimeter (p-value < 0.001). Histologic type remained independently associated with positive biopsy probability after distance adjustment (p-value < 0.001). Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC), squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) with perineural invasion (PNI), other poorly differentiated carcinomas (OPDC), and mesenchymal malignancies showed wider SLI, whereas SCC without PNI, intestinal-type adenocarcinoma (ITAC), and olfactory neuroblastoma (ONB) demonstrated limited SLI. Tissue-specific effects were generally limited, although neural tissue was associated with increased positive biopsy probability in ACC. CONCLUSIONS SLI in SNNM follows a distance-dependent pattern with the distance-invasion relationship varying according to histologic subtype. SN-based mapping represents a spatially informed strategy to enhance margin assessment and guide histology-driven surgical and radiotherapy planning. KEY POINTS Navigation-guided mapping helped to estimate microscopic tumor spread patterns. Subclinical infiltration probability decreases by approximately 5.1% per mm from the tumor margin. Histologic subtype influences the extent of microscopic local invasion. ACC showed the widest microscopic local invasion, followed by SCC with PNI. PNI increased the tumor spread in sinonasal squamous carcinoma.

Implications of the 2017 change in the French death certificate for the accuracy of mortality statistics worldwide.
abstract: BACKGROUND Differentiating between types of deaths is crucial because it allows us to better understand and prevent them, and it is essential to bringing justice to homicide victims. While there is extensive knowledge about the ways in which identifying manner of death can go wrong, the advocated solutions of more training and resources have not been put to the test. A peculiarity of the French death investigation system, along with a change in the French death certificate in 2017 allow us to test the efficacy of more specific instructions as a type of training as a solution to inaccurate information on types of deaths. METHODS Using nationwide French death certificates information available through the Epidemiological Center on Causes of Death (CépiDC) from 2016 until 2019, we conducted a before-and-after natural experiment to establish whether the 2017 change impacted the quality of mortality statistics in France. We ran logistic regression models on the likelihood that a medicolegal investigation was conducted, as well as on the quality of ICD codes for causes of death. FINDINGS The 2017 change in the French death certificate led to a two-fold increase in medicolegal investigations as well as an almost 10% increase in the quality of ICD codes of causes of death nationwide. INTERPRETATION The more specific instructions provided through the changes to the French death certificate led to improved mortality statistics, thereby providing support for the hypothesis that more training increases the quality of mortality statistics. Future research should establish dose-response, as well as focusing on policy implications beyond the French context.

title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Automated Macular Hole Diagnosis and Structured Report Generation.
abstract: INTRODUCTION Current AI models for optical coherence tomography (OCT) primarily focus on diagnosis as a standalone task. We developed and validated an end-to-end agentic AI workflow that integrates automated macular hole (MH) diagnosis from OCT images with structured patient-friendly report generation. METHODS The proposed sequential workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent consisted of an image diagnosis stage and a language generation step. The OCT version of RETFound, a self-supervised retinal foundation model, was fine-tuned for binary classification of macular OCT scans as MH or normal macula. Training, validation, and internal testing were performed using multiple public OCT datasets with patient-level stratified splitting, followed by external validation on two independent datasets. The performance of the fine-tuned foundation model was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC). For each new OCT image, the AI agent used the trained RETFound model to classify the image, received the diagnostic output, incorporated it into a structured prompt, and called the large language model (GPT-4) to generate the clinical report. RESULTS On the internal test set (n = 180), the model achieved an accuracy of 100% (95% confidence interval (CI), 97.9-100%) with an AUC of 1.00. On external validation (n = 1014), accuracy was 98.8% (95% CI 97.9-99.3%), sensitivity was 97.9% (95% CI 96.3-98.8%), specificity was 100% (95% CI 99.2-100.0%), and AUC was 0.999 (95% CI 0.998-1.000). Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analysis showed that predictions were driven by relevant retinal regions, particularly the macular hole and adjacent layers. The end-to-end agentic AI workflow generated concise and standardized patient-friendly reports for all samples, without the language model influencing diagnostic decisions. CONCLUSIONS This study demonstrates the feasibility of an end-to-end AI workflow coordinated by a workflow orchestration agent for robust OCT-based MH diagnosis with a large language model for structured report generation. By separating image-based diagnosis from language generation, this approach offers a practical and scalable solution for virtual vitreoretinal clinics.
