On MOIRAI Large, rank-16 LoRA reduces normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) by 7.5% on average while updating 3.146 million parameters, about 1% of the model, and retains most of the improvement from full fine-tuning. Chronos-2 achieves lower pretrained NMAE than MOIRAI, while its relative adaptation gains remain smaller overall. OOD results show that adaptation benefits vary by target, with the clearest gains for the local-area series and several buildings. Overall, LoRA provides a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off when adaptation yields a meaningful gain over a strong pretrained checkpoint.

title: JAXbounce: A Continuous-Control Pong-Like Benchmark for Active Inference Beyond Low Dimensional Environments
abstract: We introduce JAXbounce, a continuous control pong-like benchmark designed to evaluate active inference beyond discrete, low dimensional environments. JAXbounce combines continuous states and stochastic dynamics in discrete time with flexible and composable observation models that allow representing the environment as a state vector or a pixel grid, corruptible through the rich family of noise models we provide. It is fully differentiable and parallelisable in JAX. We run over 10,000 agent simulations on our environment comparing a baseline deterministic solution, to a state-based active inference agent with Unscented Kalman Filter perception and expected free energy planning, and a pixel based agent whose measurement model is a pretrained neural network encoder. All agents are evaluated across three scenarios of increasing difficulty with eight different noise conditions. Our experiments characterise how performance of continuous state agents scales with planning, planning horizons, observation modalities and knowledge of the noise process, exhibiting preference-oriented behaviour even in the presence of increasing uncertainty. We release JAXbounce as a reproducible benchmark for continuous control active inference research.

title: Norm-optimal model order reduction in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.

title: DiffRMST: A GPU-Accelerated Fully Differentiable Rectilinear Minimum Spanning Tree Wirelength Model for Global Placement
abstract: Analytical global placement requires a differentiable wirelength objective that accurately reflects routed interconnect cost. The widely used half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) is efficient but overlooks the internal topology of multi-pin nets. The rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT) provides higher fidelity, but its underlying decision problem is NP-complete, and its discrete construction precludes direct use in gradient-based optimization. The rectilinear minimum spanning tree (RMST) offers a polynomial-time alternative, but remains nondifferentiable because of minimization over discrete spanning trees. To address these limitations, we present DiffRMST, a fully differentiable RMST wirelength model for analytical global placement. DiffRMST combines spatial smoothing with a log-sum-exp relaxation to define a continuous distribution over spanning trees. Based on the Kirchhoff matrix-tree theorem, the partition function and edge marginals can be computed without explicit tree enumeration, enabling a closed-form topology-aware gradient for placement optimization. For efficient integration into analytical placement, we further develop a fused forward-backward operator with parallel CPU and GPU implementations. On the ISPD2019 benchmark suite, our method reduces RMST, RSMT, and routed wirelength by an average of 5.0%, 3.2%, and 3.5%, respectively, compared with the weighted-average baseline, while maintaining acceptable runtime. Furthermore, the GPU implementation achieves an average $14.7\times$ speedup in global placement over its eight-thread CPU counterpart.

title: Geometry-Aware Block Selection for Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes
abstract: Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGPs) are a widely used, principled approach to scalable Gaussian process modelling. Their success stems from their theoretically interpretable structure: they provide a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the full GP while allowing scal- able stochastic optimization. Recent work has explored modifications of the posterior conditional distribution and has shown that such extensions can improve upon this well-established framework. In particular, introducing a block-diagonal structured scal- ing matrix leads to a tighter lower bound on the GP marginal likelihood. We investigate whether selecting blocks that tighten the variational objective improves test RMSE and NLL at a fixed inducing-point budget. Since the scaling matrix contributes to the variational lower bound through an upper bound on the log-determinant of the full residual covariance matrix, our work makes the following contributions. First, we introduce a simple, scalable, geometry-aware algorithm, with explicit computational complexity and low computational overhead, that recovers a large fraction of this log- determinant contribution by selecting an appropriate partition of the data. Second, we show how to train these models using a doubly stochastic optimization framework. Finally, we investigate how sparse GP methods based on alternative conditional posterior structures can be used to learn better hyperparameters and inducing points for SVGP.

title: Bayesian nonparametric mixtures of asymmetric Archimedean copulas
abstract: Archimedean copulas are exchangeable: a single generator parameter controls every pairwise association, and the copula is invariant under permutations of its arguments. Even when mixtures of Archimedean copulas are formulated, the exchangeability feature is inherited. Non exchangeable copulas can be defined through the Khoudraji transformation of an Archimedean copula. This relies in replacing the arguments by a power transformation and adding a factor based on the independence copula. The construction produces pairwise Kendall tau coefficients that depend on the power parameters and recovers the original Archimedean copula as a particular case. We propose a Bayesian nonparametric mixture model by mixing over the copula generator parameter and the parameters that characterize the asymmetry. We use the Poisson--Dirichlet process as a mixing distribution, which groups observations by both strength and direction of dependence. We derive the copula density, the pairwise association measures, the tail coefficients, and the full posterior conditional distributions to perform a Bayesian analysis. We carry out simulation studies and real data analyses. The results show that the Khoudraji mixture improves greatly on, or agrees with, the exchangeable fit.

title: RPolyPlan: A Unified Global Floorplanning and Legalization Framework for Rectilinear Soft Modules
abstract: Floorplanning with rectilinear soft modules improves area utilization and wirelength by allowing modules to adapt to rectilinear polygon (RPoly) shapes. Existing methods typically construct rectilinear polygons through incremental refinement after obtaining a rectangular global solution, which confines polygon exploration to the neighborhood induced by the initial floorplan. This paper presents RPolyPlan, a unified framework for outline-free and fixed-outline floorplanning that directly incorporates continuously deformable rectilinear polygons into global floorplanning. To enable direct polygon optimization, we introduce a structured continuous representation and a differentiable polygon shaping model that dynamically optimizes rectilinear module shapes based on overlaps, making continuous shape optimization feasible for gradient-based global floorplanning. An augmented Lagrangian formulation robustly handles the coupled inequality constraints, provides theoretical convergence guarantees, and reduces dependence on manual penalty-parameter tuning. During legalization, minimum-cost flow and rectangular decomposition determine the target areas of subrectangles, and horizontal and vertical constraint graphs encode their geometric relations. The resulting convex legalization formulation satisfies the area, shape, separation, connectivity, and outline constraints while minimizing either the chip area or the displacement from the global floorplanning solution. Experiments on the GSRC, MCNC, and ICCAD 2023 contest benchmarks demonstrate that RPolyPlan reduces HPWL over the evaluated state-of-the-art methods by 7% and 6% in fixed-outline and outline-free experiments, respectively.

title: Diversity, Efficiency, and Incentives in Political Prediction Markets
abstract: Critics of political prediction markets argue that prices are biased because traders are not representative of voters. We test this claim by analyzing data from political betting markets spanning more than 100 years. Our analysis yields two main findings: (1) Acros markets, traders were not representative of the voters. (2) Prices were not biased by political preferences of participants. For the 2024 election, we analyzed anonymized data from Kalshi, a CFTC-regulated exchange, the largest regulated political prediction market in the U.S. Kalshi's traders were 86% male and half were under 30. In its first month of listing election contracts, Kalshi's prices were more accurate than every poll-based forecast in the national race, the seven battleground states, and nineteen Senate races, and no poll-based forecast would have been profitable to trade against them in any group of presidential contests. Its volume came from areas that voted 28% Republican, while 60% of volume went to Republican positions. Traders with a single trade placed 73% of their volume on Harris. The association between a trader's location and the direction of positions declines with trading activity and is zero among active traders, who account for most of the volume. Prices can be accurate with unrepresentative traders when the forecasts of profit-motivated traders do not depend on their demographics. Two other markets corroborate our findings. In New York's 1900 market, bettors were older than the population and drawn from finance. On PredictIt in 2016, which limited each trader to $850 per contract, positions followed registered party more closely, as our theory predicts when market restrictions do not allow profit-motivated traders to set the price. Prediction market efficiency is driven by financial incentives over demographic representativeness.

title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
abstract: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst-case interactions. With GPT-OSS-120B agents on robot routing, a three-agent team finds collision-free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six-agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

title: Improved automatic speech-based cognitive assessment using neuropsychologically calibrated diagnostic labels
abstract: Although automatic detection of cognitive impairment from conversational speech is a promising way, it becomes less accurate, as large real-world datasets often contain unreliable diagnostic labels due to self-referral and limited clinical verification, and here we investigated whether neuropsychologically calibrated diagnostic relabeling improves it. We analysed 138 hours of conversational speech from 720 participants, recalibrating unreliable diagnostic labels using attention, executive function, and memory performance via external clinical thresholds, Gaussian, and normative z-score calibration. Transformer-based classifiers were trained using both original and recalibrated labels and evaluated internally on 150 clinically verified participants and externally on Pitt, ADReSS and PROCESS-2 datasets. Memory- and MoCA-based z-score calibration produced the greatest improvements. Using our internal dataset, $F_1$ increased from $0.70$ to $0.83$ ($+13\%$) and from $0.54$ to $0.66$ ($+12\%$) for binary and multiclass classification, respectively. For external validation, the increases are $+4\%$, $+5\%$ and $+9\%$ on Pitt, ADReSS and PROCESS-2 corpus. Neuropsychologically calibrated relabeling substantially improves speech-based cognitive assessment, highlighting label quality, rather than model architecture, as a critical bottleneck in clinical AI for dementia screening.

title: ABACUS: A Benchmark for Image Editing Models to Assess Object Category and Counting Under Scene Conservation
abstract: Instruction-based image editing models can now add, remove a specified number of objects or change their category while preserving the scene. Yet these models often fail to produce the correct number, and these failures grow sharply as scenes become more complex and the requested count increases. Current benchmarks largely miss this problem: they score edits with holistic similarity metrics or with vision-language model (VLM) judges that are themselves poor at counting, so numerical errors go unnoticed or are graded incorrectly. As a result, the true numerical ability of today's editing models has never been accurately measured. We address this issue with ABACUS, a new benchmark, evaluation protocol and dedicated scoring metric for numerical image editing. Our protocol is judge-free: no VLM or MLLM scores an edit or counts objects (a VLM only confirms the category of rare ambiguous crops). Instead, it verifies each edit at the instance level against panoptic ground truth confirmed by detector consensus, checking both that the exact requested count was achieved and that the rest of the scene was preserved, across the add, remove and change operations. By evaluating leading image editors, our method reveals substantial numerical editing failures that worsen with increasing scene complexity and object count; failures that prior benchmarks often overlooked or misjudged.

title: Stabilizing Filters for Graph Signal Generation
abstract: Generating graph signals is an important task in machine learning, and incorporating the underlying graph into a generative model enables structurally-informed distribution modeling. However, said graph is often noisy or imperfectly estimated, and structural errors can affect the generative process and the resulting signal distribution. While recent work has established stability guarantees for graph neural ordinary differential equations, the robustness of graph-aware reference dynamics, as used in topological Schrödinger bridge models, remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the structural stability of continuous-time generative models whose dynamics combine a graph filter with a learned graph neural network. We first derive a Wasserstein stability bound that quantifies the effect of graph perturbations on the generated signal distributions. Informed by this analysis, we then propose a principled framework for designing graph filters that balance structural stability with induced signal smoothing. We characterize the optimal filter design and provide an explicit family of polynomial filters with provable stability guarantees. Experiments on synthetic graphs and real-world fMRI signals support our theoretical findings, illustrating the enhanced structural stability of the proposed filters while preserving generative performance.

title: Manifold-Informed Neural Networks for Low-Label ECG Electrolyte Inference
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_φ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_φ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

title: Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
abstract: Factual sycophancy, a language model's deference to a user's false beliefs, is usually understood as a bid for the user's approval at the expense of truthfulness. We argue that this framing over-emphasizes the user and propose viewing sycophancy as a failure within the broader and generally useful process of in-context updating, by which models revise their answers based on information supplied during an interaction. We support this view with behavioral and mechanistic evidence. First, models' responses to user claims sit within a broader pattern of source-sensitive updating. They revise their answers in response to information attributed to external sources as well, more so when it appears better supported, and their deference to the user persists even when no user approval is at stake. Second, the internal components that support deference to the user are also causally important for in-context updating more broadly. Our results suggest that factual sycophancy arises when in-context updating gives a user's assertion excessive weight relative to its evidence. Because sycophancy is embedded in this process, reducing it risks reducing useful updating as well, a trade-off that calls for evaluations measuring both behaviors and mitigations that decouple them.

title: Economic resources, sporting efficiency and uncertainty: a global test on the 2026 FIFA world cup
abstract: A related paper (arXiv:2610.06967) developed a stochastic optimization framework in which football performance combines GDP/population-based potential with a latent mean-reverting efficiency process. The framework was applied to a cross-section of the 24 national teams participating in AFCON 2025. This paper applies the same methodology to the full 48-team 2026 FIFA World Cup, extending the analysis beyond Africa without modifying the underlying model. Using GDP, population, FIFA ranking data, and complete tournament outcomes, it evaluates the framework against a global sample spanning all six confederations. Two findings emerge. First, GDP and population explain only 9 percent of single-tournament performance variance, compared with 33 percent for FIFA points. This gap is consistent with the model's distinction between systematic performance and match-specific idiosyncratic shocks. Second, using the less noisy FIFA-points measure, the African pattern persists globally: Morocco, Senegal, Argentina, Croatia, Portugal, and Uruguay emerge as leading GDP-relative over-performers. Conversely, several major economies, including the United States, Germany, Japan, and South Korea, underperform their GDP-implied potential. As in the related paper, we interpret the residual as a symmetric, non-structurally identified conditional performance residual, rather than an SFA-consistent efficiency estimate. We also quantify the extent to which its cross-country variance mechanically reflects the underlying performance measure. The GDP-rank/simulated-performance-rank correlation is robust to the choice of the model's unidentified dynamic parameters across a wide grid.

title: TexFlow: learning crystallographic texture on SO(3) manifold via normalizing flows
abstract: Crystallographic texture is an important microstructural feature that statistically describes the orientations of grains in polycrystalline materials. Conventional texture analysis relies on the orientation distribution functions and pole figures, which are essential for interpreting the texture of a given material specimen but do not, by themselves, provide a direct framework for predictive modeling of process-structure-property linkages. Data- and machine learning-based approaches offer a means to address this gap; however, a key challenge lies in developing representations and learning frameworks that account for the manifold structure of rotations. In particular, many existing machine learning techniques are designed for Euclidean data and therefore are not readily applicable to rotations in the non-Euclidean group $\text{SO}(3)$. Here we introduce TexFlow, a conditional normalizing flow framework for texture modeling that learns a probability distribution over rotations in $\text{SO}(3)$ by construction. Rotations are encoded in a six-dimensional Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization representation which is then mapped back to valid rotations $\mathbf{R}\in\text{SO}(3)$. The framework supports conditional probabilistic modeling of texture $p(\mathbf{R}|c)$, where $c$ may represent processing parameters like temperature or deformation state. To complement conventional texture-analysis visualizations, such as pole figures and sections of the orientation distribution function, we further introduce Hopf-fibration visualizations as a compact global representation of texture. TexFlow is validated on both unconditional and conditional experimental and simulated texture datasets spanning diverse material systems. We show that TexFlow can accurately capture multimodal textures and their conditional evolution, providing a data-driven framework for establishing process-texture linkages.

title: Topology-Adaptive Seismic Response Prediction of Interconnected Structural Systems Using Reduced Order Model Embedded Graph Neural Network
abstract: Electrical substation equipment is commonly interconnected by busbars and flexible conductors. Such interconnected infrastructures exhibit complex dynamic interactions, where the response of each component is influenced by local structural properties, mechanical coupling, system topology, and transient excitation. High-fidelity FE models can capture some of these effects, but their computational cost limits their use for real-time prediction. Purely data-driven models offer faster inference, yet they struggle to generalize, requiring additional simulations and retraining for each new configuration. This work presents a ROM embedded Graph Neural Network (ROMeGNN) for topology-aware seismic digital twins of interconnected structural systems. The system is represented as a graph, where structural components are treated as nodes and mechanical interconnections as edges. Each high-fidelity component model is first reduced to a reduced-order modal representation, which forms a differentiable dynamics operator within the GNN. Rather than learning the full response directly, the GNN estimates topology-dependent interaction forces that enter the differentiable ROM solver as coupling inputs for modal state advancement. This hybrid formulation preserves the known component-level physics and uses data-driven message passing to learn complex inter-component forces across varying system layouts. The framework is demonstrated on interconnected electrical substation equipment subjected to randomized seismic inputs. It delivers rapid predictions of response quantities relevant to seismic damage assessment while remaining applicable across varying layouts, component combinations, and excitation scenarios. These results highlight the potential of embedding physics within graph learning architectures for real-time, interpretable, topology-adaptive seismic digital twins of interconnected engineering systems.

title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution
abstract: Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.

title: Beyond Trajectory Statistics: Community-Consistent Human Mobility Generation via Evolving User-Location Graphs
abstract: Human mobility data are fundamental to Web-based location services and broader urban applications, and mobility generation provides synthetic trajectories when real data are costly or inaccessible. Although recent mobility generators have incorporated collective mobility patterns, they primarily focus on individual trajectories and aggregate population dynamics, leaving evolving community structures formed by user-location interactions insufficiently modeled. In this paper, we study community-consistent human mobility generation. To this end, we formulate mobility generation as the generation of dynamic user-location graphs to model community structures and propose MOTION, a Multi-agent framework for cOmmuniTy-consIstent human mObility geNeration. MOTION consists of user agents, location agents, and a global manager agent. MOTION first detects coherent communities from historical mobility using the Leiden algorithm and extracts community-conditioned interaction priors to guide the generation process. Guided by these priors, the user agents plan mobility, search destination candidates, and infer user movements from the individual view. In parallel, selectively activated location agents infer likely user arrivals from the community view. The manager coordinates both views, diagnoses interactions causing deviations, and attributes targeted reflection signals to revise user decisions, location attraction, and source-user selection. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that MOTION outperforms baselines by at least 4.05% across reported metrics of individual trajectories, population and flow distributions, and community and graph structures. Further analyses confirm its robustness, privacy preservation, and downstream utility. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION-04C4.

title: Claims of emergence in AI should be grounded in information decomposition
abstract: When a language model develops capabilities not traceable to its individual components, when a multi-agent AI system outperforms each agent on its own, or when a human-AI pair succeeds where either fails in isolation, AI researchers describe it as a case of ``synergy'' or ``emergence''. However, these are usually informal assessments not supported by a theoretical framework, making these claims impossible to compare or even meaningfully dispute. Here we argue that \emph{information decomposition can serve as a unifying formal framework to operationalize assessments about synergy in AI systems}. Information decomposition provides a way to distinguish qualitatively different \emph{types} of information, including unique information available from individual components, redundant information shared across multiple components, and synergistic information accessible only from parts taken together. This gives claims of emergence a precise, falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. We apply this lens to attention heads, autonomous agents, and human-AI teams, showing how it organizes existing knowledge across scales and substrates, while also generating cross-level conjectures that siloed fields would miss.

title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.

title: Proof-Carrying Contracts: Commitments AI Agents Cannot Break
abstract: AI agents increasingly act on behalf of people or other agents, purchasing services, exchanging information and delegating work. What an agent must respect is written in instructions, policies or agreements, but text alone cannot make it comply. It may make mistakes, be redirected by what it reads, or pursue different interests. For an economy of such agents to function, parties need agreements they can rely on without inspecting or trusting one another's agents. We introduce Proof-Carrying Contracts (PC2), a framework for making agreed constraints enforceable throughout an agent's interactions with a system. Before a requested operation can run, the agent must supply a machine-checkable proof that it preserves the agreed constraints in every case allowed by its model. An execution system called the Airlock checks the proof and controls access to the operation. The parties specify the conditions to preserve, while the agent supplies the reasoning needed to justify its decisions and remains free to adapt its strategy. This avoids having to design a separate permission policy and prove that every decision it permits is safe. We prove that the constraints hold at every instant during execution, even for an adversarial agent, and identify when this implies safety in the world. Reusable capability modules provide tools and guarantees from which contracts can be constructed. PC2 provides a foundation for an agent economy whose agreements protect both those delegating work and those carrying it out.

title: Model- and Layer-Level Closed-Loop Forecasting with SSM-Based Spiking Neural Networks
abstract: Deep State-Space Models (Deep SSMs) have shown promising performance and computational benefits in processing of time-series data with complex temporal dependencies. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) constitute a biologically inspired class of deep SSMs, where computing blocks communicate through spikes, discrete single-bit events rather than continuous activation functions. A particularly important task in time-series processing is forecasting, i.e. predicting future values of a sequence from past observations alone. However, how to best perform forecasting with SNNs is an open question, where the standard autoregressive nature of the data processing with SNNs requires values that are not available during the forecasting phase. In this article, we address this challenge. We explore two closed-loop forecasting strategies, in which the network's own generated values are fed back into the network as if they were observed past values: (i) model-level and (ii) layer-level closed-loop forecasting. We evaluate these approaches on the ETT-small datasets, a standard benchmark for time-series forecasting, under both spike-based and continuous activation functions. We compare the proposed closed-loop approaches against state-of-the-art methods such as SpaceTime, as well as the zero-masking baseline in S4. Both of the proposed approaches perform comparably to or better than zero-masking with S4, and in most cases match SpaceTime. These findings highlight the trade-off between continuous and low-bit quantized activations, and demonstrate that the proposed Deep SSM architectures provide a competitive framework for forecasting.

title: TracePrism: Extending Semantic Trace Topics to Iterative, Encoding-Aware Trace Partitioning
abstract: Process mining typically explains an event log with a single model, clustering, or classifier fitted to all cases, although real logs often mix cases that follow different sub-processes. Trace clustering separates sub-populations, but it fixes one notion of trace similarity for the whole analysis. We propose TracePrism, which treats process discovery as iterative partitioning with three characteristics. The trace encoding is adaptive: it is chosen for each working set of remaining traces from a library of encodings, with suggestions scored for that set. The partitioning is iterative: the analyst forms a candidate group based on a rule, a dominant topic, a cluster over topic weights, or a region of an embedding, accepts it if it is coherent in both process structure and outcome, and continues with the remaining traces. Decisions are revisable and recorded: a group can be reopened under a different working set or encoding, and the findings repository keeps both the earlier decision and its revision. We implement TracePrism as an open-source prototype and demonstrate it in usage scenarios on three real-world event logs. The scenarios also revealed behavior that we had not anticipated, such as process drift.

title: TOI-3686: A Hot Jupiter and Sub-Neptune In A 2:1 Mean-Motion Resonance
abstract: Hot Jupiters are typically thought to be "lonely", but a small and growing subset of them have been found to have nearby planets in the same system. We present the discovery of a new member of this class of systems, TOI-3686. TOI-3686 c is a hot Jupiter with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 5.078$ days detected by NASA's TESS mission that shows peak-to-peak transit timing variations (TTVs) of 40 minutes, amongst the largest ever observed for a hot Jupiter. A subsequent search of the TESS data revealed the transits of a second planet, TOI-3686 b, a sub-Neptune with $P_\mathrm{orb} = 2.54$~days and peak-to-peak TTVs of 10 hours, $\sim 16\%$ of its orbital period. We characterized the system through photodynamical modeling of photometry from TESS and ground-based facilities, as well as radial velocity measurements from the NEID and MAROON-X spectrographs. We find that the two planets in the TOI-3686 system are deep in a 2:1 mean-motion resonance, making this the only hot Jupiter system currently known to be in a truly resonant configuration, which may be related to its $\lesssim1$~Gyr system age. Systems like TOI-3686 likely formed through a dynamically quiescent pathway and were captured into resonance after migration through a disk, and may represent the high-mass end of processes that occur in compact systems of smaller planets.

title: Discount Yourself: Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip for Decentralised Learning under Client Outages
abstract: Decentralised federated learning (DFL) trains personalised models on devices that average with their neighbours rather than with a central server. Real devices, however, are often offline for hours or days, and a client returning from an outage can recover only by aggregating the models its neighbourhood holds. We observe that the stalest of these models is usually the client's own, a case that existing staleness-aware rules, which discount only the models a client receives, do not address. We formalise aggregation after an outage as estimating the state of a fully available network and derive three principles. First, the receiver must be discounted like any neighbour. Every rule that weights it at least as much as each neighbour has an error that grows without bound with the outage, whereas discounting all candidates by relative staleness keeps the error bounded. Second, staleness must be measured as inherited lag rather than age, since local training resets a model's age but not the lag it absorbed from stale neighbours. We introduce the effective lag, which tracks this quantity at the cost of one scalar per message. Third, the discount must be steep, because absorbed lag persists in every later round. These principles define Self-inclusive Freshness-weighted Gossip (SFG), a family of drop-in aggregation rules with the communication and computation of decentralised federated averaging, whose guarantees hold for the stale receiver itself. On three image benchmarks and eight outage processes, including real smartphone availability traces, the lag-based members SFG-L and SFG-Cut consistently outperform decentralised federated averaging and recent age-of-information rules, and ablations show that each principle is necessary. The analysis also explains why tuned limited merging from gossip learning is effective.

title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

title: Differentiable powder X-ray diffraction enables analysis of evolving structures
abstract: Operando and in-situ experiments extend powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) to materials that evolve during experiments, producing series of hundreds or thousands of patterns. Such series are commonly refined one pattern at a time, so weak signals give noisy structural trajectories. Parametric refinement instead fits a shared model to all patterns, but with most existing programs, changing the model or fitting it efficiently remains challenging. Here, we introduce diffPXRD, a differentiable PXRD engine in PyTorch. diffPXRD calculates derivatives by automatic differentiation, so a shared model can be changed without new derivative code. Batched fitting is also more than seven times faster than serial fitting. In an operando cathode series, a shared lattice model can reduce lattice-parameter variability by 68.4% when 10% of the photon counts are retained. We also show shared models can describe the precipitation and dissolution of Li2S and reconstruct collective atomic displacements in Ca3Ti2O7.

title: A Comparative Study of LED Lighting Control Strategies for Energy-Efficient Greenhouse Operations
abstract: Greenhouse supplemental lighting is essential for meeting crop Daily Light Integral (DLI) requirement. However, conventional always-on and rule-based strategies are inherently energy-inefficient since they ignore future sunlight availability. This paper reports the results of deploying various supplemental lighting control strategies, namely, always-on, always-off, heuristic, optimal prediction-based, and two peak-shift variants, simultaneously in a single greenhouse at the Hampton Roads AREC of Virginia Tech, to ensure that every treatment experiences identical conditions. %The shared infrastructure is built on an MQTT-based IoT platform with Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density (PPFD) sensing and PWM-driven LED control; The prediction-based and peak-shift strategies optimize LED schedules using a Markov chain-based solar forecast. Experimental results over two replicates %(20~February--15~April~2026, 72~plants per treatment) show that the prediction-based strategy meets the desired DLI target at 65\% cost reduction relative to the always-on baseline while achieving the highest dry-mass yield among the proposed adaptive strategies. The heuristic strategy incurs only a 6\% cost premium over prediction-based control, offering a competitive forecast-free alternative. The peak-shift variants achieve the lowest active-strategy costs by shifting LED demand into off-peak tariff windows. A yield-per-dollar efficiency metric is finally introduced to jointly capture energy cost and crop output showing that the prediction-based strategy ranks highest at 18.976~g/\$, more than double the always-on value of 9.391~g/\$. These findings can provide greenhouse operators with an evidence-based framework for selecting a lighting control approach that balances energy cost, crop quality, and system complexity.

title: Continuous-Time Policy Gradient from Discrete Data: Convergence Analysis and Model-Free Algorithms
abstract: Continuous-time reinforcement learning seeks an optimal policy under unknown dynamics driven by stochastic differential equations using observations collected at discrete times. We develop a policy gradient framework that combines rigorous convergence analysis with learning from discrete data. We first establish a performance difference lemma and derive policy gradient formulas for randomized and parametrized policies. We then prove exponential convergence of an entropy-regularized policy flow to the regularized optimum. For discrete parametrized updates, we derive a convergence bound that explicitly separates the contributions of critic error, policy-regression error, and the learning step size. To enable learning under unknown dynamics, we integrate this framework with PhiBE, which constructs a continuous-time surrogate generator from discrete transition data. The resulting on-policy and off-policy model-free actor-critic algorithms preserve the continuous-time structure of the control problem. Numerical experiments on an entropy-regularized linear-quadratic regulator and a nonlinear wheeled robot demonstrate the performance and stability of the proposed methods with both known and data-driven dynamics.

title: Beyond the Sequentiality Bottleneck: A Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
abstract: Autoregressive models (ARMs) face a "Sequentiality Bottleneck" in reasoning, while diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallelism but lack semantic coherence. To addresses both limitations, we propose Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning (CoRAL), a hybrid framework via an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture: a DLM Planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while a large ARM Executor selects the optimal plan and synthesizes the final answer. To train the Planner effectively, we introduce Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer it toward goal-directed reasoning. Experiments on vision-language benchmarks show that CoRAL significantly outperforms prior diffusion-based methods and achieves competitive performance against strong ARMs, achieving both superior efficiency and quality.

title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

title: AEON: Unifying Video and 3D World Models
abstract: Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives---specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)---as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON

title: Gravothermal Evolution of Self-Interacting Dark Matter Halos across Knudsen Numbers
abstract: If the dark matter self-interacts elastically via a light mediator, then at relative velocities above a scale $w$ dictated by particle physics parameters, the cross section scales as $σ\propto v^{-4}$. Depending on the value of $w$, the self-interaction cross section in low-mass halos could be (much) larger than has been previously studied extensively. We perform kinetic simulations of isolated self-interacting dark matter halos using the code KiSS-SIDM for a wide range of halo masses, concentrations, and cross sections from $50 \,\mathrm{cm}^2 \, \mathrm{g}^{-1}$ to $250{,}000 \, \mathrm{cm}^2 \, \mathrm{g}^{-1}$, including several velocity-dependent and fully differential (anisotropic) cross sections. We demonstrate that for idealized NFW halos the collapse time can be predicted from the Knudsen number at the scale radius of the halo. We perform similar calculations for halos extracted from cosmological simulations using either $N$-body (collisionless) or SPH (strongly collisional) dynamics, and then evolve cutouts with KiSS-SIDM. For these halos, the collapse times differ from the idealized NFW simulations by up to a factor of a few. Further, we calibrate a hydrostatic fluid model to these results, which solves the structure equations as a boundary value problem via two-point shooting. The fluid calculation predicts that for velocity-independent cross sections, a convective region of the halo develops late in the collapse. The collapse times agree well between the kinetic simulations and the fluid code, especially in the velocity-independent case. The density profiles agree well in some cases, which include all of the velocity-dependent cross section runs.

title: PIANISTpy: A JAX-based Python package for velocity-anisotropic astrophysical equilibrium models
abstract: The hierarchical assembly of dark matter haloes and galaxies via mergers and anisotropic mass accretion naturally imprints non-trivial velocity anisotropy onto haloes and galaxies, an empirical fact emerging from cosmological simulations. However, dynamical studies based on idealised numerical simulations typically assume isotropic velocity distributions for the systems studied. This is mainly because no tools exist to construct anisotropic initial conditions with fully self-consistent (i.e., physical and instability-free) truncation boundary conditions for finite spatial extents. Here we present the first such analytical framework that performs truncation in phase space, with two distinct approaches to guarantee either the monotonicity of output distribution functions or identical truncated density profiles. We additionally present the open-source JAX-based GPU-accelerated Python package PIANISTpy (Particle Initial conditions with ANISoTropy) for constructing spherical, non-rotating initial conditions, supporting arbitrary double-power-law analytical radial density profiles and a library of analytical anisotropy profiles. This framework further permits the construction of systems with non-analytical anisotropy profiles via an arbitrary linear superposition of all implemented analytical anisotropy models as basis functions. PIANISTpy also outputs 3D velocity profiles and line-of-sight-integrated observables with end-to-end differentiability for rapid gradient-based Monte Carlo inference, and self-consistent local dark matter velocity distributions of anisotropic haloes beyond the unphysical Maxwell-Boltzmann simplification adopted in terrestrial detection experiments. We discuss use cases and demonstrate PIANISTpy's orders-of-magnitude higher numerical solver accuracy and superior dynamical stability of particle initial conditions relative to existing tools, including galpy and AGAMA.

title: Where Do Legal Factors Live in LLMs?
abstract: In case-based legal reasoning, legal professionals identify legally significant fact patterns in a new dispute and compare them with those of decided cases. In AI & Law, HYPO dimensions and CATO factors represent these patterns symbolically, organizing expert knowledge distilled from case narratives as explicit, structured, interpretable, and auditable legal concepts and relations that support case comparison, legal argument, and precedent-based reasoning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for legal tasks, yet their internal organization of legal knowledge remains difficult to trace. We investigate whether LLMs form internal representations corresponding to all 26 CATO factors. Two research questions examine linear decodability and sparse localization with sparse autoencoders. Experiments cover three open models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2 2B, supported by cross-model comparison and human audit of controlled natural-language passages. Results show that all 26 factors are linearly decodable in all three models. Single-feature sparse readouts cover the complete factor catalog, with best-layer test AUCs ranging from 0.86 to 1.00. Five selected features approach full-vector readout performance. We report 78 model-specific layer-feature coordinates, one for each factor in each model. Together, these results show that information corresponding to expert-defined legal factors can be read from the internal activations of LLMs processing legal narratives. By locating these readouts, our study connects legal language and the symbolic abstractions of HYPO and CATO to learned internal representations.

title: A Mechanistic Study of Automated Failure Attribution in LLM-based Agentic Systems
abstract: Agentic systems have demonstrated strong capabilities on complex tasks by enabling multiple interacting large language model (LLM)-based agents to collaborate and execute subtasks in parallel. However, this collaborative structure introduces new challenges for reliably evaluating and diagnosing system failures, particularly failure attribution: tracing a system's execution to identify the agent step responsible for an incorrect final outcome. Because manually performing this task is time- and labor-intensive, recent work has turned to LLMs as judges to automate the process, referred to as automated failure attribution (AFA). These approaches assume that a sufficiently capable model can infer the failing step directly from an interaction transcript. In practice, however, direct prompting often performs poorly, which motivates follow-up work that explores various ways to improve AFA performance, including alternative prompting strategies and inference-time interventions. In this paper, we examine a more fundamental question: whether this weak behavioral performance reflects a genuine capability limitation. Using linear probes applied to internal activations, we uncover a significant \emph{knows-but-won't-say gap:} models encode sufficient information to attribute a failure correctly but fail to explicitly output the responsible step. Building on this finding, we propose \emph{grafting}, a simple manual intervention that exploits knowledge already encoded in the model to improve AFA performance without requiring ground-truth labels at inference time. Extensive evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmark settings demonstrate that grafting consistently outperforms direct-prompting approaches, underscoring the potential of leveraging latent model knowledge for more reliable failure attribution. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/mi4afa.

title: Brittle by Design? Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems
abstract: As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective.

title: Register Anything Model for Generalizable and Robust Point Cloud Registration
abstract: We present Register Anything Model (RAM), a unified model for generalizable 3D point cloud registration that robustly estimates 6-DoF transformations across diverse domains spanning sensors and environments. Existing registration methods are typically tailored to a single domain, with carefully tuned architectures and hyperparameters, and thus degrade markedly when applied to novel domains. We bridge this gap by training a single model on diverse data from indoor, outdoor, and object domains. A central challenge is the severe geometric discrepancy across domains, i.e., differences in scene scale, sensor noise, point density, and structural patterns, which hinders processing with a unified point-based model. To address this, we introduce a geometry-aware normalization strategy that jointly voxelizes and normalizes point clouds into a standardized geometric space, adaptively based on their geometric properties to preserve salient local structures while standardizing resolution. Built on this normalization, RAM follows a hierarchical coarse-to-fine paradigm, and employs an efficient geometric transformer that models local geometric consistency instead of globally over all points. This design mitigates discretization noise introduced by voxelization, and improves computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on 12 benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of inlier ratio and registration recall. Notably, our method outperforms the counterparts trained on each separate domain, showing superior generalization capability.

title: Self-Supervised Tuning of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models via High-Fidelity Feedback
abstract: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.

title: DualHeads: Reward-tilted few-step diffusion made simple
abstract: Distilled diffusion models generate high-quality images in a few sampling steps, but aligning them with task requirements and human preferences is difficult. Methods developed for multi-step diffusion models rely on differentiable rewards, or on score fields and stochastic trajectories that distilled generators may lack. We ask whether a few-step generator can be adapted using only external reward evaluations and reference samples, and show that two binary classifiers suffice. Our method, DualHeads, implements them as lightweight heads on a frozen diffusion backbone. The reward head learns which samples of the same prompt score higher, the reference head separates reference images from generated ones, and the generator maximizes a weighted sum of their logits. When the heads are optimal, this objective is KL-regularized maximization of the learned reward, and the ratio of head weights sets the regularization strength. Empirically, with both rule-based and model-based rewards, a few-step DualHeads generator reaches task rewards close to those of 40-step reinforcement learning methods while preserving image quality, at no extra inference cost. We hope that this simple and elegant dual-head formulation will help advance few-step reward-tilted generation.

title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
abstract: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.

title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
abstract: Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet-ai/fig.

title: Mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted model of sedimentation
abstract: A model for the consolidation-sedimentation process incorporating thermal effects is analysed. The model is motivated by novel applications to heat-assisted sedimentation of mineral suspensions. A system of convection-diffusion equations for the concentration and temperature are coupled to flow equations for the volume-average velocity and pressure. The model is supplemented with Dirichlet and mixed boundary conditions. A quasi-stationary approach of the system is analysed by means of a mixed variational formulation, where additional variables such as the pseudostress tensor and variables for the gradient of the temperature and concentration are introduced. The existence and uniqueness of the system is shown making use of the Babu{\v s}ka-Brezzi theory and Banach's fixed-point theorem, under hypotheses of smallness of the data and additional regularity on the solutions. A discrete formulation based on finite element spaces is proposed and analysed, and the existence of solutions is achieved thanks to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. Additionally, Céa and a priori estimates are derived for the mixed formulation. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the performance of the model and to confirm the theoretical rates of convergence.

title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

title: Scriptorium: System Design and Implementation of a Multi-Human, Multi-AI Collaborative Digital Library Search Platform
abstract: This technical report documents the design and implementation of Scriptorium, a digital library search interface designed to support multi-human, multi-AI collaboration: full cross-user transparency of search activity combined with a Manager--Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. A companion short demonstration paper describes Scriptorium's interaction design; because a demonstration format is constrained to a few pages, it necessarily omits most implementation detail. This report documents Scriptorium's complete system architecture, data model, collaborative-interaction design rationale, and AI orchestration mechanism, including verbatim agent prompts, the deterministic guardrails that constrain them, the language model and retrieval configuration, and the steps needed to run the system, so that the design can be inspected, critiqued, reproduced, and reused by other researchers. We also discuss the system's current limitations and the user study we are planning to evaluate its central hypothesis: that combining collaborative transparency with scoped multi-agent AI assistance increases serendipitous cross-pollination between collaborators' research threads.

title: The Data Differentiator Framework (DDF): Quantifying Marginal Data Value with Information-Theoretic and Game-Theoretic Measures in an Agentic Evaluation Pipeline (SDSAE)
abstract: In data-rich enterprises the hard question is not whether a candidate dataset is good in isolation, but whether it adds information beyond what the organization already holds, and whether that increment is worth its price. We present the Data Differentiator Framework (DDF), a composite scoring method for candidate data assets that combines (i) a mutual-information-based redundancy penalty against the existing portfolio, (ii) a cost-normalized, significance-gated marginal utility score derived from an ablation study, and (iii) explicit governance inputs (trust, identity resolution quality, strategic weights) set by the business. The framework is executed by a staged pipeline, the Strategic Data Sourcing Agent Ecosystem (SDSAE), that short-circuits expensive model-retraining steps for assets failing governance or redundancy gates. Conceptually, the DDF extends the relevance-minus-redundancy principle of mRMR feature selection from the feature level to the asset level, and adds cost normalization, a statistical significance gate, and governance terms that per-sample valuation methods such as Data Shapley do not model. We validate the framework on the public credit-card fraud benchmark (284,807 transactions) with five constructed candidate assets spanning the redundancy spectrum.
